cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe saprotrophic nutrition
cards.oldBack: The process by which an organism obtains its nutrients by secreting digestive enzymes onto organic matter from dead or decaying organisms and then absorbing the resulting simple nutrients.
cards.newFront: Describe saprotrophic nutrition (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Organism secretes digestive enzymes onto dead or decaying organic matter
  • Enzymes break down large insoluble molecules into small soluble molecules (extracellular digestion)
  • Simple nutrients are then absorbed into the organism

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Define cytoplasm (3 points)
cards.oldBack:
A jelly-like substance that
- contains all the organelles of the cell
- contains dissolved nutrients and salts
- is where most of the cell’s chemical reactions take place.
cards.newFront: Give 3 features of cytoplasm
cards.newBack:
• Jelly-like substance filling the cell
  • Contains organelles, dissolved nutrients and salts
  • Site where most chemical reactions take place (controlled by enzymes)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe the nucleus
cards.oldBack: An organelle found in most eukaryotic cells that contains the genetic material of the cell and controls the activities of the cell. {3 exceptions: red blood cells, sieve tube (phloem) and some eye}
cards.newFront: Describe the nucleus (2 functions)
cards.newBack:
• Contains the cell’s genetic material (DNA / chromosomes)
  • Controls the activities of the cell
  • Found in eukaryotic cells (exceptions: red blood cells, phloem sieve tube cells)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Define ribosomes
cards.oldBack: {non-membranous} organelles that are the site of protein synthesis.
cards.newFront: Define ribosomes
cards.newBack: Non-membranous organelles that are the site of protein synthesis.

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What as an active site, and how can its shape be affected?
cards.oldBack:
Part of the enzyme that is complementary to the shape of the substrate. The
shape of the active site may change if the enzyme is exposed to high temperatures or
extremes of pH.
cards.newFront: What is an active site, and what can change its shape?
cards.newBack:
• Region of an enzyme with a specific shape complementary to its substrate
  • Shape changes permanently (denatures) at high temperatures or extremes of pH

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Define osmosis
cards.oldBack: The diffusion of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from an area with more water (lower solute concentration) to an area with less water (higher solute concentration).
cards.newFront: Define osmosis (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Net movement of water molecules
  • From a region of higher water potential (dilute solution) to lower water potential (concentrated solution)
  • Across a partially permeable membrane

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Define surface area to volume ratio, and describe why it's important.
cards.oldBack:
The amount of surface area per unit volume of an object.

It determines how efficiently substances can enter or leave a cell or organism, affecting processes like diffusion, heat transfer, and nutrient uptake.
cards.newFront: Define surface area to volume ratio and why it matters
cards.newBack:
• The surface area per unit volume of an object or organism
  • Larger SA:V ratio gives faster exchange of substances (O2, CO2, nutrients, heat) by diffusion
  • Large organisms have a small SA:V ratio, so need a transport system

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What is the alimentary canal? Name its major parts.
cards.oldBack: The continuous digestive tube running from the mouth to the anus, containing the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum and ileum) and large intestine (colon and rectum)
cards.newFront: What is the alimentary canal? Name its main parts in order.
cards.newBack:
Continuous muscular tube from mouth to anus:
  • Mouth → oesophagus → stomach
  • Small intestine (duodenum & ileum)
  • Large intestine (colon, rectum & anus)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What is bile?
cards.oldBack:
A green, watery fluid made in the liver and stored in the gallbladder that is used to
neutralise stomach acid in the duodenum and emulsify fats.
cards.newFront: What is bile?
cards.newBack:
A green, watery fluid made in the liver and stored in the gallbladder that is used to
neutralise stomach acid in the duodenum and emulsify fats.

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: State the word equation for anaerobic respiration in muscles
cards.oldBack: glucose ⟶ lactic acid + energy
cards.newFront: State the word equation for anaerobic respiration in muscles
cards.newBack: glucose ⟶ lactic acid + energy

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What is coronary heart disease and what's the link to smoking?
cards.oldBack:
A disease caused by the build-up of fatty deposits inside the
coronary arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow to the heart tissue. Smoking
increases the risk of coronary heart disease.
cards.newFront: What is coronary heart disease, and how does smoking affect it? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Fatty deposits build up inside the coronary arteries
  • Arteries narrow, reducing blood flow (and O2) to heart muscle
  • Smoking increases the risk of coronary heart disease

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Define phagocyte
cards.oldBack:
A type of white blood cell (in the immune system) that engulf/absorb and destroy pathogens, dead cells, and debris.

They are essential for defending the body against infections and keeping tissues healthy.
cards.newFront: Define phagocyte (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• A type of white blood cell in the immune system
  • Engulfs and digests (destroys) pathogens by phagocytosis

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What are coordination centres? Give three examples.
cards.oldBack:
Areas of the body that receive and process information from receptors, and send signals to effectors to produce a response. 

e.g. brain, spinal cord, pancreas
cards.newFront: What are coordination centres? Give three examples.
cards.newBack:
Areas of the body that receive and process information from receptors, and send signals to effectors to produce a response.

e.g. brain, spinal cord, pancreas

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What are effectors?
cards.oldBack: Muscles or glands that receive signals from a coordination center and produce a response that helps restore homeostasis and maintain optimal internal conditions.
cards.newFront: What are effectors?
cards.newBack: Muscles or glands that receive signals from a coordination centre and produce a response that helps restore homeostasis and maintain optimal internal conditions.

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Define insulin
cards.oldBack: A hormone secreted by the pancreas when blood glucose concentration is too high. It reduces blood glucose concentration.
cards.newFront: Define insulin
cards.newBack: A hormone secreted by the pancreas when blood glucose concentration is too high. It reduces blood glucose concentration.

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What does oestrogen do and where it is produced?
cards.oldBack:
The main female reproductive hormone responsible for the growth and repair of the uterus lining, and the development of secondary sexual characteristics in females.

Released by the ovaries.
cards.newFront: Where is oestrogen produced and what are its 2 main roles?
cards.newBack:
• Produced by the ovaries
  • Causes repair and thickening of the uterus lining
  • Controls female secondary sexual characteristics

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What are receptors?
cards.oldBack: Organs or cells that detect stimuli and send signals to coordination centers. E.g. photoreceptors in the eyes
cards.newFront: What are receptors?
cards.newBack: Organs or cells that detect stimuli and send signals to coordination centers. E.g. photoreceptors in the eyes

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe testosterone
cards.oldBack: The main male reproductive hormone produced by the testes. It stimulates the production of sperm and is responsible for the development of male secondary sexual characteristics.
cards.newFront: Where is testosterone produced and what are its 2 main roles?
cards.newBack:
• Produced by the testes
  • Stimulates sperm production
  • Controls male secondary sexual characteristics

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Define allele
cards.oldBack: A specific version of a gene that determines a particular trait. For example, if a gene determines eye color, one allele might code for blue eyes and another for brown eyes.
cards.newFront: Define allele
cards.newBack:
• A different version (form) of the same gene
  • Example: alleles for eye colour (blue vs brown)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What is mitosis, and in which biological processes (3 or 4) does it play a key role?
cards.oldBack:
A form of cell division that produces two genetically identical daughter cells - with a full set of chromosomes.

Mitosis is involved in repair, growth, cloning and asexual reproduction.
cards.newFront: Define mitosis and give 3–4 processes that use it
cards.newBack:
• Cell division producing two genetically identical diploid daughter cells
  • Used for growth, repair of damaged tissues, cloning and asexual reproduction

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What are decomposers and what do they do?
cards.oldBack: Organisms that release enzymes to break down dead plant and animal material into simpler organic matter (saprotrophic nutrition), thereby recycling nutrients like nitrogen back into the soil.
cards.newFront: What are decomposers and what do they do? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Organisms (bacteria and fungi) that feed by saprotrophic nutrition
  • Secrete enzymes to break down dead organic matter
  • Recycle mineral ions (e.g. nitrates) back into the soil and CO2 into the air

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What are producers?
cards.oldBack: Organisms, typically plants or algae, that produce their own food (e.g. through photosynthesis), forming the base of the food chain.
cards.newFront: What are producers?
cards.newBack: Organisms, typically plants or algae, that produce their own food (e.g. through photosynthesis), forming the base of the food chain.

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What are tertiary consumers?
cards.oldBack: Predators that eat secondary consumers, often at the top of the food chain, and are typically not preyed upon by other organisms.
cards.newFront: What are tertiary consumers?
cards.newBack: Predators that eat secondary consumers, often at the top of the food chain, and are typically not preyed upon by other organisms.

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What is eutrophication?
cards.oldBack:
Pollution of water by fertiliser leading to excessive growth of algae at the
water surface. This prevents light reaching aquatic plants, causing them to die, and reduces
the amount of oxygen available for animal species.
cards.newFront: Describe the stages of eutrophication (4 points)
cards.newBack:
• Excess fertiliser (nitrates) leaches into water → rapid algal bloom
  • Algae block light → underwater plants cannot photosynthesise and die
  • Decomposers (bacteria) feed on dead plants and respire aerobically
  • Oxygen runs out → fish and aquatic animals die

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What is leaching and what can it cause?
cards.oldBack: The loss of plant nutrients from the soil when fertilisers run off the land into lakes and rivers. This may be due to rain or irrigation and can lead to eutrophication.
cards.newFront: What is leaching and what can it cause?
cards.newBack:
• Rain or irrigation washes soluble mineral ions / fertilisers out of soil into rivers and lakes
  • Can trigger eutrophication

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What are genetically modified (GM) crops?
cards.oldBack:
Crops that have had their genomes modified by the insertion of a desired gene
from another organism.
cards.newFront: What are genetically modified (GM) crops?
cards.newBack:
Crops that have had their genomes modified by the insertion of a desired gene
from another organism.

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What 8 characteristics do all living organisms share?
cards.oldBack:
MRS C GREN
- Movement
- Respiration
- Sensitivity (response to surroundings)
- Control (of internal conditions)
- Growth and development
- Reproduction
- Excretion of waste
- Nutrition
cards.newFront: What 8 characteristics do all living organisms share? (MRS C GREN)
cards.newBack:
• Movement · Respiration · Sensitivity
  • Control of internal conditions
  • Growth & development · Reproduction
  • Excretion · Nutrition

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Give 3 differences between plant and animal cells
cards.oldBack:
- Plant cells have a cell wall whereas animal cells do not

- Plant cells have a permanent vacuole whereas animal cells do not

- Plant cells have chloroplasts and are able to photosynthesise whereas animal cells do not
cards.newFront: Give 3 structures found in plant cells but not animal cells
cards.newBack:
• Cell wall (made of cellulose)
  • Permanent vacuole (filled with cell sap)
  • Chloroplasts (for photosynthesis)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Give two different species of bacteria
cards.oldBack:
Lactobacillus bulgaricus - Used in the production of yoghurt from milk.
Pneumococcus - Bacterium that causes pneumonia.

Also: streptococcus, staphylococcus, E. coli, salmonella
cards.newFront: Give 2 named examples of bacteria from the specification
cards.newBack:
• Lactobacillus bulgaricus — rod-shaped; used to make yoghurt from milk
  • Pneumococcus — spherical; pathogen that causes pneumonia

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Give 4 biotic factors that affect communities
cards.oldBack:
Any of these:
- Number of predators
- Food availability and competition
- Disease
- Human activity
- Parasitism
- Presence of pollinating insects
- Availability of nest sites
cards.newFront: Give 4 biotic factors that affect communities
cards.newBack:
• Predators (predation)
  • Food availability and competition
  • Disease and parasitism
  • Human activity · pollinating insects · nest sites

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What detrimental impacts can sulfur dioxide have on the environment?
cards.oldBack:
Sulfur dioxide can dissolve in water to form acid rain:
  • Kills animals (by making the lakes in which they live in acidic)
  • Damages plants and buildings
  • Causes respiratory problems in humans and cause acid rain.
cards.newFront: What are the harmful effects of sulfur dioxide? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
Dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain:
  • Makes lakes acidic, killing fish and aquatic life
  • Damages plants/trees and erodes limestone buildings
  • Causes respiratory problems in humans

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Why are biomass transfers not 100% efficient? (4 things)
cards.oldBack:
Energy is lost through for example:
- Egestion (removal of faeces)
- Excretion (removal of waste products e.g. urine)
- Respiration
- The production of inedible bones and shells
cards.newFront: Give 4 reasons why energy transfer between trophic levels is not 100% efficient
cards.newBack:
• Respiration (heat lost to surroundings)
  • Egestion (undigested food lost as faeces)
  • Excretion (waste such as urine)
  • Inedible / uneaten parts (bones, shells, roots)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
What is the difference between a food
web and a food chain?
cards.oldBack:
Food chains show one path of food dependencies. Food webs show the interactions of
multiple different food chains.
cards.newFront:
What is the difference between a food
web and a food chain?
cards.newBack:
Food chains show one path of food dependencies. Food webs show the interactions of
multiple different food chains.

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: How are new genes introduced into an organism?
cards.oldBack:
- The organisms genes are cut using restriction enzymes to create sticky ends
- The DNA from a bacterium is also cut to produce sticky ends
- The gene is inserted into the bacterium and joined together by DNA ligase enzymes
cards.newFront: How is a new gene inserted into a bacterial plasmid? (3 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Cut out the desired gene using restriction enzymes (leaving sticky ends)
  • Cut open a bacterial plasmid with the same restriction enzyme
  • Join the gene into the plasmid using DNA ligase to form recombinant DNA

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Draw a graph to show how the rates of photosynthesis and respiration are affected by light intensity over a day
cards.newFront: Draw a graph to show how the rates of photosynthesis and respiration are affected by light intensity over a day
cards.newBack:
• Respiration stays roughly constant day & night
  • Photosynthesis is 0 in the dark, rises at dawn, peaks at midday (max light), and falls to 0 at dusk

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe the structure of an alveolus
cards.oldBack: - Small sacs with capillaries around them that serve as the gaseous exchange surface.
cards.newFront: Describe the structure of an alveolus
cards.newBack:
• Tiny air sacs surrounded by dense capillaries — site of gas exchange (O2 into blood, CO2 out)
  • 1-cell-thick wall, moist lining, huge surface area

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: How does smoker’s cough arise?
cards.oldBack:
Cilia in the trachea move mucus containing dirt and microbes out of the lungs.

Smoking damages or destroys these cilia.

Mucus builds up in the lungs, causing irritation and leading to smoker’s cough as the body tries to clear it.
cards.newFront: How does smoker’s cough arise? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Cilia normally sweep mucus (trapping dust & microbes) out of the airways
  • Chemicals in smoke damage or destroy the cilia
  • Mucus builds up, causing irritation and coughing to clear it

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: How does increased temperature increase the crop yield?
cards.oldBack:
Higher temperatures increase enzyme activity, speeding up reaction (e.g. in photosynthesis) and growth, which boosts crop yield.

However, if the temperature exceeds the optimum, enzymes denature, reducing yield.
cards.newFront: How does increasing temperature affect crop yield in a glasshouse? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Higher temperature increases enzyme activity → faster photosynthesis and growth
  • Above the optimum, enzymes denature and yield falls

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: How does a continuous supply of carbon dioxide increase the crop yield?
cards.oldBack:
- CO2 is needed for photosynthesis which isneeded to provide energy for growth

- Without a constant supply of enough CO2, it may become a limiting factor and so the rate of photosynthesis is slower
cards.newFront: How does extra CO<sub>2</sub> increase crop yield in a glasshouse? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• CO2 is a reactant for photosynthesis, making glucose for growth
  • Supplying extra CO2 prevents it becoming a limiting factor, keeping the rate high

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe how yoghurt is made from milk
cards.oldBack:
- Bacteria (Lactobacillus) is used to break the lactose in milk down into lactic acid

- Lactic acid lowers the pH of the milk which causes proteins to denature and makes the
milk turn into yoghurt
cards.newFront: Describe how yoghurt is made from milk (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Add Lactobacillus bacteria to pasteurised milk
  • Bacteria respire anaerobically, converting lactose → lactic acid
  • Lactic acid lowers the pH, denaturing milk proteins so the milk thickens into yoghurt

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Label this diagram of a fermenter
cards.newFront: Label this diagram of a fermenter
cards.newBack:
• Nutrients in (top right) · Gases out (top left)
  • Mixing blades / paddles (stir contents evenly)
  • Water jacket (keeps temperature at optimum) · Products out (bottom)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What is the difference between asexual reproduction and sexual reproduction?
cards.oldBack:
• Asexual reproduction involves mitosis, producing genetically identical offspring from a single parent.
  • Sexual reproduction involves meiosis, producing genetically different offspring by combining male and female gametes (sperm and egg), forming a zygote.
cards.newFront: Compare asexual and sexual reproduction (2 key differences)
cards.newBack:
• Asexual: 1 parent, uses mitosis, produces genetically identical offspring (clones)
  • Sexual: 2 gametes fuse (fertilisation) after meiosis, forming a zygote and genetically different offspring

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
Give one advantage and one
disadvantage of asexual reproduction
cards.oldBack:
Advantage - It produces lots of offspring quickly
Disadvantage - It does not introduce variation and so all offspring are susceptible to the same environmental pressures as the parents.
cards.newFront: Give 1 advantage and 1 disadvantage of asexual reproduction
cards.newBack:
• Advantage: produces many offspring quickly from one parent (no mate needed)
  • Disadvantage: no genetic variation, so all offspring are vulnerable to the same disease or environmental change

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
Describe the process of fertilisation in
plants
cards.oldBack:
- Pollen grain lands on the stigma
- Pollen tube begins to grow from the pollen grain into the ovary
- Pollen grain travels down the pollen tube and fertilizes the egg
- Fruit and seeds form from the egg
cards.newFront: Describe fertilisation in flowering plants (4 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Pollen grain lands on the stigma
  • A pollen tube grows down the style into the ovary
  • The male gamete (pollen nucleus) travels down the tube and fuses with the egg cell in the ovule
  • Fertilised ovule → seed; ovary → fruit

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: State three secondary sexual characteristics associated with testosterone.
cards.oldBack:
- Growth and development of the penis, testes and pubic hair
- Deeper voice
- Increased muscle mass
cards.newFront: State three secondary sexual characteristics associated with testosterone.
cards.newBack:
- Growth and development of the penis, testes and pubic hair
- Deeper voice
- Increased muscle mass

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
Describe the effect of temperature on the
rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction
cards.oldBack:
- As the temperature increases, so does the rate of reaction
- Once the temperature exceeds the optimum, the enzyme denatures and the rate of reaction decreases
cards.newFront:
Describe the effect of temperature on the
rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction
cards.newBack:
• Rate increases up to the optimum temperature (more kinetic energy → more frequent collisions)
  • Above optimum, rate drops steeply because the active site denatures

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Why does the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increase when the temperature increases?
cards.oldBack:
- As the temperature increases the particles have more kinetic energy
- This increases the chance of collisions between molecules being successful and leading to a reaction
cards.newFront: Why does enzyme reaction rate increase as temperature rises (up to the optimum)? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Particles gain more kinetic energy and move faster
  • Leads to more frequent successful collisions between enzymes and substrates

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
Describe the effect of pH on the rate of
an enzyme-controlled reaction
cards.oldBack:
- The rate of an enzyme catalysed reaction is fastest at the optimum pH
- If the pH is too high or low, the enzyme will work less efficiently and the active site may be denatured at extremes of pH
cards.newFront: Describe the effect of pH on enzyme activity (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Rate is fastest at the optimum pH
  • At extremes of pH (too acidic or too alkaline), the active site changes shape (denatures) so the substrate no longer fits

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What are the 5 main parts to a coordinated response?
cards.oldBack:
- A stimulus (e.g. temperature change)
- A receptor (to detect the change)
- A coordinator (to decide what happens)
- An effector (to carry out the response)
- A response (e.g. withdrawing hand)
cards.newFront: What are the 5 parts of a coordinated response in order?
cards.newBack:
• Stimulus (change in environment)
  • Receptor (detects stimulus)
  • Coordinator (e.g. brain / spinal cord)
  • Effector (muscle or gland)
  • Response (action carried out)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
What is phototropism and which part of a
plant is positively phototropic?
cards.oldBack:
Phototropism is a plant’s directional growth response to light. The shoots are
positively phototropic (they grow towards
the light source).
cards.newFront:
What is phototropism and which part of a
plant is positively phototropic?
cards.newBack:
Phototropism is a plant’s directional growth response to light. The shoots are
positively phototropic (they grow towards
the light source).

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
How does auxin cause the shoots to
grow towards the light source?
cards.oldBack:
- Auxin collects on the shaded side
- Auxin promotes cell growth: triggers growth of the main stem more on the shaded side (and inhibits the growth of side shoots).
- The shoot curves towards the light
cards.newFront: How does auxin make a plant shoot grow towards light? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Auxin collects on the shaded side of the shoot
  • Auxin stimulates more cell elongation on the shaded side
  • The shaded side grows longer, making the shoot bend towards the light

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
Give 3 differences between nervous and
hormonal communication
cards.oldBack:
- Nervous communication uses nerve cells and impulses whereas hormones are secreted by glands and travel in the blood

- Nervous communication is generally much faster than hormonal communication

- Hormonal communication usually brings about longer lasting responses than nervous communication
cards.newFront: Give 3 differences between nervous and hormonal communication
cards.newBack:
• Transmission: electrical impulses along neurones vs chemical hormones in the blood
  • Speed: nervous is very fast vs hormonal is slower
  • Duration: nervous is short-lived (localised) vs hormonal is longer-lasting (widespread)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe the reflex arc
cards.oldBack:
- Stimulus detected by a receptor
- Impulse passed along sensory neurone to a relay neurone (in the CNS)
- Impulse passed along motor neurone to effector
- Effector brings about the response
cards.newFront: Describe the pathway of a reflex arc (4 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Stimulus detected by a receptor
  • Impulse travels along a sensory neurone to a relay neurone (in CNS)
  • Impulse passes along a motor neurone to an effector
  • Effector carries out the rapid, automatic response

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
Describe the sequence of events
involved in removing a hand away from a
hot flame
cards.oldBack:
- Receptors in the hand detect the heat of the flame
- An impulse is sent along a sensory neurone
- The impulse passes through relay neurones (in the CNS)
- The impulse then passes along a motor neurone and triggers the muscles in the arm to move the hand away
cards.newFront: Describe the reflex arc when pulling your hand from a hot flame (4 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Temperature receptors in skin detect heat
  • Impulse travels along a sensory neurone → relay neurone (spinal cord / CNS)
  • Impulse travels along a motor neurone to arm muscles (effector)
  • Muscles contract, pulling the hand away

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
How does the eye respond to bright
light?
cards.oldBack: The iris contracts, making the pupil smaller and letting in less light
cards.newFront:
How does the eye respond to bright
light?
cards.newBack: The iris contracts, making the pupil smaller and letting in less light

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What is adrenaline and where is it released from?
cards.oldBack:
A hormone produced in response to fear or stress as part of the ‘fight or flight’ response

Released from the adrenal glands
cards.newFront: What is adrenaline and where is it released from?
cards.newBack:
A hormone produced in response to fear or stress as part of the ‘fight or flight’ response

Released from the adrenal glands

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Give 3 effects of adrenaline in the body
cards.oldBack:
- Increases heart and breathing rate
- Increases blood glucose concentration
- It boosts blood flow to the brain and muscles and away from the digestive system.
- Dilates the pupils
cards.newFront: Give 3 effects of adrenaline on the body
cards.newBack:
• Increases heart rate and breathing rate
  • Increases blood glucose concentration (for respiration)
  • Diverts blood flow to muscles and brain (away from gut) · dilates pupils

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe translocation
cards.oldBack: Translocation is the movement of sugars and amino acids up and down the plant from source ( i.e. leaves) to the sink areas (e.g. roots and growing tissues)
cards.newFront: Describe translocation in plants (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Movement of sucrose and amino acids through the phloem
  • Moves both up and down from sources (leaves) to sinks (roots, growing points, storage organs)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
Describe the double circulatory system in
mammals
cards.oldBack: The heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, the oxygenated blood returns to the heart and is then pumped around the body.
cards.newFront:
Describe the double circulatory system in
mammals
cards.newBack: The heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, the oxygenated blood returns to the heart and is then pumped around the body.

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe the structure of arteries
cards.oldBack: A blood vessel with thick, muscular, elastic walls and a narrow passageway that carries blood away from the heart under high pressure to the rest of the body.
cards.newFront: Describe the structure of arteries
cards.newBack:
• Thick muscular & elastic walls to withstand high pressure
  • Narrow lumen · carries blood away from the heart (no valves)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe the structure of capillaries
cards.oldBack: Thin, narrow blood vessels (about one cell thick) to allow for the easy exchange of substances between blood and tissues.
cards.newFront: Describe the structure of capillaries
cards.newBack:
• Walls one cell thick → very short diffusion distance
  • Tiny lumen allowing easy exchange of O2, glucose and CO2 between blood and tissues

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe the structure of veins
cards.oldBack: Veins have less muscle and elastic tissue than arteries and they have a larger passageway as the blood is at lower pressure, they also have valves to prevent backflow.
cards.newFront: Describe the structure of veins (3 features)
cards.newBack:
• Thinner walls (less muscle and elastic tissue than arteries)
  • Wide lumen — carries blood at low pressure
  • Contain valves to prevent backflow of blood

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
Describe the blood flow through the right
side of the heart
cards.oldBack:
- Deoxygenated blood flows into the right atrium from the vena cava

- This blood passes through the right AV valve into the right ventricle

- The blood is then pumped out of the heart to the lungs through the right SL valve and into the pulmonary artery
cards.newFront: Describe blood flow through the right side of the heart (3 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium via the vena cava
  • Passes through the right AV valve into the right ventricle
  • Pumped through the semilunar valve into the pulmonary artery → lungs

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
Describe the blood flow through the left
side of the heart
cards.oldBack:
- Blood enters into the left atrium from the pulmonary vein

- The blood is then pumped through the left AV valve into the left ventricle

- The blood is then pumped out through the left SL valve and into the aorta
cards.newFront: Describe blood flow through the left side of the heart (3 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Oxygenated blood enters the left atrium via the pulmonary vein
  • Passes through the left AV valve into the left ventricle
  • Pumped through the semilunar valve into the aorta → body

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Why does the heart rate increase during exercise?
cards.oldBack:
- More muscle movement requires more energy from respiration

- The muscle tissues need to be provided with a supply of oxygen to carry out respiration and so the heart needs to pump faster to provide the oxygen
cards.newFront: Why does heart rate increase during exercise? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Contracting muscles need more energy from aerobic respiration
  • Heart pumps faster to deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles
  • Also removes carbon dioxide faster

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
Explain the effect of temperature on the
rate of photosynthesis
cards.oldBack:
- As temperature increases, so does the rate of photosynthesis

- Once the temperature exceeds the optimum, the rate of photosynthesis decreases as enzymes begin to denature
cards.newFront: Explain the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Up to the optimum: rate increases (more kinetic energy → more frequent enzyme–substrate collisions)
  • Above the optimum: rate drops sharply because enzymes denature

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What is the inverse square law for light intensity?
cards.oldBack:
The inverse square law states that as the distance (d) from a light source increases, the light intensity (I) decreases proportionally to the square of the distance.
\[ I \propto \frac{1}{d^2} \]
E.g. if the distance doubles, the light intensity quarters.
cards.newFront: State the inverse square law for light intensity
cards.newBack:
I ∝ 1d2
  • Light intensity (I) is inversely proportional to distance squared (d2)
  • If distance doubles, light intensity quarters (÷ 4)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe the structure of leaf tissue. (Name the five layers and state where guard cells are found)
cards.newFront: Describe the structure of leaf tissue. (Name the five layers and state where guard cells are found)
cards.newBack:
• Top → bottom: waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, lower epidermis
  • Guard cells sit in the lower epidermis, opening and closing the stomata

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
What is the difference between the
alimentary canal and the digestive
system?
cards.oldBack:
The alimentary canal is the continuous tube that food passes through (mouth, oesophagus, etc.)

The digestive system includes the alimentary canal plus digestive glands and organs like the liver, pancreas, and salivary glands, which aid digestion.
cards.newFront: What is the difference between the alimentary canal and the digestive system?
cards.newBack:
• Alimentary canal: the continuous tube food passes through (mouth → anus)
  • Digestive system: the alimentary canal plus associated glands/organs (salivary glands, liver, pancreas)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: How is the ileum adapted for absorption?
cards.oldBack: The ileum is lined with villi which provide a large surface area for reabsorption
cards.newFront: How is the ileum adapted for absorption?
cards.newBack:
• Lined with millions of finger-like villi (with microvilli) for a huge surface area
  • 1-cell-thick wall (short diffusion distance), dense capillary network (glucose/amino acids), and lacteal (fatty acids/glycerol)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: When is an organism described as heterozygous?
cards.oldBack: An organism is heterozygous for a gene if it has two different alleles, like Bb. The dominant allele usually determines the trait, but the recessive allele can still be passed to offspring.
cards.newFront: What does heterozygous mean? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Having two different alleles for a gene (e.g. Bb)
  • The dominant allele is expressed in the phenotype, while the recessive allele can still be passed on

Draw a Punnett square for a cross
between a homozygous recessive blue
eyed female (bb) with a heterozygous
brown eyed male (Bb)
cards.newFront:
Draw a Punnett square for a cross
between a homozygous recessive blue
eyed female (bb) with a heterozygous

cards.newBack:

  • 50% Bb (brown eyes) · 50% bb (blue eyes)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront:
Draw a Punnett square for a cross
between a homozygous dominant red
flower (RR) with a homozygous
recessive white flower (rr)
cards.newFront:
Draw a Punnett square for a cross
between a homozygous dominant red
flower (RR) with a homozygous
recessive white flower (rr)
cards.newBack:
RR
rRrRr
rRrRr
  • 100% Rr (all heterozygous, all red flowers)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What is random fertilisation?
cards.oldBack:
• The random process by which any sperm can fertilise any egg.
  • Since each sperm and egg carry different genetic material, this increases genetic variation in offspring.
cards.newFront: What is random fertilisation and why does it matter?
cards.newBack:
• Any sperm can fuse with any egg by chance
  • Because gametes carry different combinations of alleles, this increases genetic variation

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe the process of natural selection
cards.oldBack:
- Populations are naturally varied due to random genetic mutations
- Some of these mutations provide a selective advantage
- These organisms survive and reproduce, passing on the successful genes
cards.newFront: Describe the stages of natural selection (4 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Variation exists within a population due to random mutations
  • Some individuals have an allele giving a selective advantage
  • They are more likely to survive and reproduce
  • They pass on the advantageous allele to offspring (frequency increases over generations)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Describe how antibiotic resistance arises
cards.oldBack:
- A random genetic mutation causes a bacterium to become resistant to the antibiotic
- When the antibiotic is used, all the bacteria that do not have the mutation are killed
- The population containing just the resistant bacteria then begins to grow
cards.newFront: How does antibiotic resistance evolve in bacteria? (4 steps)
cards.newBack:
• A random mutation makes some bacteria resistant to the antibiotic
  • When the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed
  • Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce rapidly (less competition)
  • The resistance allele is passed on → population becomes resistant

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What are lipids made of? Give two examples of lipids.
cards.oldBack: Lipids include fats and oils.
cards.newFront: What are lipids made of? Give two examples of lipids.
cards.newBack:
• Built from 1 glycerol molecule joined to 3 fatty acids
  • Contain the elements carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
  • Examples: fats (solid at room temp, e.g. butter) and oils (liquid, e.g. olive oil)

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: How do you test for glucose?
cards.oldBack:
Grind into powder, add Benedict's solution (blue), heat gently.

It will change colour depending on glucose concentration
(low → high) green → yellow → orange → red
cards.newFront: How do you test for glucose (reducing sugar)?
cards.newBack:
• Add Benedict’s solution (blue) and heat in a water bath
  • Colour change (low → high glucose): green → yellow → orange → brick-red precipitate

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: How do you test for starch?
cards.oldBack: Grind into powder, add iodine solution (brown), gently shake → Blue-black if starch is present.
cards.newFront: How do you test for starch?
cards.newBack: Grind into powder, add iodine solution (brown), gently shake → Blue-black if starch is present.

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Why do plants need nitrates and what happens when they are deficient?
cards.oldBack: Plants need nitrates to make amino acids for proteins for growth. Without them, plants grow poorly and leaves turn yellow.
cards.newFront: Why do plants need nitrates and what happens when they are deficient?
cards.newBack:
• Use: nitrates provide nitrogen to make amino acids and proteins for growth
  • Deficiency: stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Why do plants need phosphates and what happens when they are deficient?
cards.oldBack: Plants need phosphates for respiration and growth, and to make DNA and cell membranes. Without them, roots grow poorly, and leaves turn purple.
cards.newFront: Why do plants need phosphates and what happens when they are deficient?
cards.newBack: Plants need phosphates for respiration and growth, and to make DNA and cell membranes. Without them, roots grow poorly, and leaves turn purple.

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Why do plants need potassium and what happens when they are deficient?
cards.newFront: Why do plants need potassium and what happens when they are deficient?
cards.newBack:
• Use: needed to help enzymes involved in photosynthesis and respiration
  • Deficiency: poor flower and fruit growth and discoloured/yellow leaves with dead spots

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Why do plants need magnesium and what happens when they are deficient?
cards.oldBack: Plants need magnesium for chlorophyll for photosynthesis. Without it, leaves turn yellow (but veins stay green)
cards.newFront: Why do plants need magnesium and what happens when they are deficient?
cards.newBack:
• Use: needed to make chlorophyll (for photosynthesis)
  • Deficiency: yellow leaves (chlorosis) and slow growth

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: Label the image and explain how germination happens
cards.newFront: Label parts 1–4 of the seed and explain how germination happens
cards.newBack:
• 1: Seed coat (testa) · 2: Embryo shoot · 3: Embryo root · 4: Food store
  • Seed absorbs water → enzymes digest food store (starch) into glucose for respiration, releasing energy for the embryo to grow
  • Once green leaves emerge above soil, the plant makes its own food by photosynthesis

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: State the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast
cards.oldBack: Glucose → Ethanol + Carbon dioxide + Energy
cards.newFront: State the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast
cards.newBack: Glucose → Ethanol + Carbon dioxide + Energy

cards.subject: biology
cards.oldFront: What is a Punnett square?
cards.oldBack: A grid used to predict the possible genetic outcomes of a cross between two organisms. It shows how alleles from each parent combine to determine traits in the offspring.
cards.newFront: What is a Punnett square used for?
cards.newBack:
• A genetic diagram grid showing how alleles from two parents combine at fertilisation
  • Used to predict the probabilities / ratios of offspring genotypes and phenotypes

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you investigate the effect of temperature on amylase activity? (4 points)
cards.newBack:
• Keep starch + amylase in a water bath at each test temperature (allow time to equilibrate)
  • Every 30 s, drop a sample onto iodine solution in a spotting tile
  • Record time until iodine stays orange-brown (no longer blue-black — all starch digested)
  • Shortest time = fastest rate (optimum temperature); control pH, enzyme & starch volumes/concentrations

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you investigate osmosis using potato cylinders and Visking tubing?
cards.newBack:
• Living (potato): weigh equal cylinders, place in different sucrose concentrations, blot dry & reweigh; calculate % change in mass = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100
  • Non-living (Visking tubing): artificial partially permeable membrane filled with sucrose solution in water → water enters by osmosis, level rises

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you test a leaf for starch safely? (4 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Destarch plant in the dark for 48 h before the experiment
  • Boil leaf in water (kills cells & softens membranes)
  • Heat in ethanol in a hot water bath (no naked flame — ethanol is flammable) to remove chlorophyll
  • Rinse in warm water, then add iodine solution → blue-black if starch is present

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you test that photosynthesis requires light, CO<sub>2</sub> and chlorophyll (and produces O<sub>2</sub>)?
cards.newBack:
• Light: cover part of a leaf with foil (only uncovered part turns blue-black)
  • Chlorophyll: use a variegated leaf (only green parts turn blue-black)
  • CO2: place leaf in flask with soda lime / NaOH to absorb CO2 (stays orange-brown)
  • O2 evolved: count bubbles / collect gas from pondweed → relights a glowing splint

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: How do human energy requirements vary with activity level, age and pregnancy? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Activity level: more active people need more energy for muscle contraction
  • Age: children/teenagers need more energy per kg for growth; requirements decrease in older age
  • Pregnancy: pregnant women need extra energy to support the growing fetus

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Where is bile made and stored, and what are its 2 roles in digestion?
cards.newBack:
Made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, released into the small intestine:
  • Alkaline — neutralises stomach HCl to give the optimum pH for intestinal enzymes
  • Emulsifies lipids into tiny droplets — increases surface area for faster lipase digestion

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: What is the role of ATP in living cells?
cards.newBack:
• ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the immediate energy carrier produced by respiration
  • Provides energy for muscle contraction, active transport, cell division and building large molecules

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: State the word equations for anaerobic respiration in animals and in plants/yeast
cards.newBack:
• Animals: glucose → lactic acid
  • Plants & yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you show respiring seeds release heat and CO<sub>2</sub>? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Heat: place germinating seeds in an insulated vacuum flask with a thermometer (cotton wool bung lets gas exchange)
  • Control: boiled (dead) seeds washed in disinfectant to kill bacteria that would also respire
  • CO2: bubble gas through limewater (turns milky) or hydrogencarbonate indicator (red → yellow)

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Give 4 ways alveoli are adapted for efficient gas exchange
cards.newBack:
• Millions of tiny sacs give a huge total surface area
  • Walls are one cell thick → very short diffusion distance
  • Dense capillary network & continuous ventilation maintain a steep concentration gradient
  • Moist lining so gases dissolve before diffusing

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you investigate CO<sub>2</sub> release and the effect of exercise on human breathing?
cards.newBack:
• CO2 test: breathe through a two-tube limewater/hydrogencarbonate apparatus — exhaled air turns limewater milky much faster than inhaled air
  • Exercise: count breaths per minute at rest vs after exercise → breathing rate and depth increase to supply more O2 and remove more CO2

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Why do large multicellular organisms need a transport system? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• They have a small surface area to volume ratio and long diffusion distances to deep cells
  • Simple diffusion alone is too slow to supply enough O2/nutrients and remove waste

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Why is responding to changes in the environment essential for organisms?
cards.newBack:
• Increases chances of survival (finding food/light, escaping predators, avoiding harmful conditions)
  • Maintains stable internal conditions (homeostasis) via nervous and hormonal coordination

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: How do plants respond to light and gravity? (2 tropisms)
cards.newBack:
Plants respond slowly by growth movements (tropisms) controlled by auxin:
  • Shoots: positive phototropism (grow towards light) & negative geotropism (grow away from gravity)
  • Roots: positive geotropism (grow towards gravity for water & anchorage)

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Core practical: what 3 conditions are needed for seed germination, and how do you test them?
cards.newBack:
Needs Water, Oxygen and Warmth (light is not needed):
  • Tube A (control): damp cotton wool, air, warm → germinates
  • Tube B (no water): dry cotton wool · Tube C (no oxygen): boiled cooled water + oil layer · Tube D (no warmth): in fridge → do not germinate

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Compare the secondary sexual characteristics controlled by oestrogen and testosterone
cards.newBack:
• Oestrogen (ovaries): breast development, wider hips, pubic/underarm hair, start of menstrual cycle
  • Testosterone (testes): deeper voice, facial & body hair, broader shoulders/muscle growth, sperm production

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: What is polygenic inheritance?
cards.newBack:
• Most phenotypic features (e.g. height, skin colour) are controlled by many genes interacting together, not a single gene
  • Produces a wide range of phenotypes (continuous variation)

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: How is human biological sex determined at fertilisation? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Females have sex chromosomes XX (all eggs carry X)
  • Males have XY (50% of sperm carry X, 50% carry Y)
  • At each fertilisation there is a 50% (1:1) chance of XX (female) or XY (male)

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you investigate anaerobic respiration in yeast? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Boil and cool the glucose solution first to remove dissolved oxygen (cool so yeast isn’t killed)
  • Add a layer of liquid paraffin / oil on top to stop oxygen entering from the air
  • Count CO2 bubbles per minute (or collect gas in a syringe) while varying temperature or sugar concentration

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Describe the steps of selective breeding in animals (4 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Choose parents with the desired characteristic (e.g. high milk yield or docile temperament)
  • Breed them together
  • Select the offspring that best show the desired trait
  • Repeat over many generations (disadvantage: reduces genetic variation / increases risk of inherited disease)

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Distinguish between excretion and egestion
cards.newBack:
• Excretion: removal of metabolic waste products made inside cells (e.g. CO2 from lungs, urea in urine)
  • Egestion: removal of undigested food (faeces) that was never absorbed into body cells

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: In the temperature & amylase core practical, why must you leave the starch and amylase tubes in the water bath for 5 minutes before mixing?
cards.newBack:
• So both solutions reach the target temperature before the reaction starts (a valid, fair test)
  • Also keep pH constant using a buffer solution

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Give 3 cellular processes that use energy transferred by ATP from respiration
cards.newBack:
• Muscle contraction (movement)
  • Active transport (pumping molecules against a concentration gradient)
  • Building large molecules (e.g. proteins from amino acids) · maintaining body temperature · cell division

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Why does anaerobic respiration release much less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration?
cards.newBack:
• Glucose is only incompletely oxidised (partially broken down without oxygen)
  • Most of the chemical energy remains locked inside lactic acid (animals) or ethanol (plants/yeast)

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: How do ventilation (breathing) and blood flow keep diffusion fast in the alveoli?
cards.newBack:
• Breathing constantly brings in fresh O2-rich air and removes CO2
  • Flowing blood carries oxygenated blood away and brings deoxygenated blood in
  • Both maintain a steep concentration gradient for rapid diffusion

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Why can a single-celled organism (like Amoeba) survive without a circulatory system?
cards.newBack:
• It has a very large surface area to volume (SA:V) ratio
  • Diffusion distance is very short, so diffusion alone is fast enough to supply O2/nutrients and remove waste

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Which organs secrete oestrogen and testosterone, and how do they travel to target tissues?
cards.newBack:
• Oestrogen: secreted by the ovaries · Testosterone: secreted by the testes
  • Both are hormones transported in the blood plasma to target organs

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Why does the father’s sperm — not the mother’s egg — determine the biological sex of a baby?
cards.newBack:
• Mother is XX, so every egg carries an X chromosome
  • Father is XY, so sperm carry either X (gives XX girl) or Y (gives XY boy) with 50% probability each

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: In the yeast anaerobic respiration practical, why do you boil the glucose solution and then let it cool before adding yeast?
cards.newBack:
• Boil: drives off dissolved oxygen so the yeast respires anaerobically
  • Cool before adding yeast: boiling water would denature the yeast’s enzymes and kill the yeast

cards.subject: biology
cards.newFront: Why is genetic variation (from mutation) essential for natural selection to happen?
cards.newBack:
• Without variation, no individuals would have an advantageous allele when the environment changes
  • Variation allows better-adapted individuals to survive, reproduce, and pass on the favourable allele

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: What is diffusion and in which substances does it occur?
cards.oldBack:
Diffusion is the process where particles spread out, moving from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration (down the concentration gradient).

It occurs in gases and liquids (solutions).
cards.newFront: Define diffusion and state which states of matter it occurs in
cards.newBack:
• Net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to lower concentration (down a concentration gradient)
  • Occurs in gases and liquids (solutions)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Describe and explain fractional distillation
cards.oldBack:
Fractional distillation separates a mixture of liquids based on their different boiling points

The mixture is heated until it vaporizes and passes into a fractionating column. The column is hot at the bottom and cool at the top - the liquids condense at different heights based on their boiling points.
cards.newFront: Describe fractional distillation (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Separates a mixture of miscible liquids with different boiling points
  • Mixture is heated until it vaporises and rises up a fractionating column (hot at bottom, cool at top)
  • Each liquid condenses at the height matching its boiling point

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
Describe and explain
filtration
cards.oldBack:
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid (within which it is suspended)

The mixture is poured onto filter paper on a funnel. The liquid (filtrate) passes through the filter paper, but the insoluble solid (the residue) is caught as pits articles are too big.
cards.newFront: Describe filtration (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Separates an insoluble solid from a liquid
  • Mixture is poured through filter paper in a funnel
  • Liquid (filtrate) passes through; insoluble solid (residue) is trapped because its particles are too large

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
Describe and explain
chromatography
cards.oldBack:
Chromatography separates a mixture of substances dissolved in a solvent based on their movement through a medium.

A piece of paper with a spot containing a mixture is placed in a beaker with some solvent. The bottom of the paper is in contact with the solvent. The solvent level slowly rises, separating the spot (mixture) into few spots (components).
cards.newFront: Describe paper chromatography (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Separates a mixture of soluble substances (e.g. dyes/inks) in a solvent
  • Spot mixture on a pencil baseline above the solvent level
  • Solvent rises up the paper, carrying components at different speeds depending on their solubility and attraction to the paper

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
What is an isotope? Do isotopes
of a certain element have the same
chemical properties?
cards.oldBack:
Atoms of the same element (same proton number) that have a different
number of neutrons.
They have the same chemical properties as they have the same
electronic structure.
cards.newFront: What is an isotope? Why do isotopes have the same chemical properties?
cards.newBack:
• Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons
  • Same chemical properties because they have the same electronic configuration (same outer-shell electrons)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
Describe the properties of noble
gases. Discuss the trend in boiling
point down the group.
cards.oldBack:
Non-metals, colourless gases at room temperature, low boiling points,
unreactive (full outer shell; they don’t easily accept or lose electrons).
The boiling point increases down the group, as the atoms get heavier.
cards.newFront: Describe the properties of noble gases (Group 0) and their boiling point trend (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Colourless, monatomic gases at room temperature with low boiling points
  • Unreactive (inert) — they have a full outer shell of electrons
  • Boiling point increases down the group as atoms get larger / intermolecular forces get stronger

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: What is ionic bonding?
cards.oldBack: Ionic bonding is the transfer of electron(s) from a metal atom to a non-metal atom to form positive and negative ions which are then strongly electrostatically attracted.
cards.newFront: Describe ionic bonding (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom
  • Forms positive metal ions and negative non-metal ions
  • Held together by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: How are ionic compounds held together?
cards.oldBack: They are held together by electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions in a giant lattice.
cards.newFront: How are ionic compounds held together?
cards.newBack: They are held together by electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions in a giant lattice.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
State properties of ionic
substances
cards.oldBack:
High melting and boiling point (strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions).

Do not conduct electricity when solid (ions in fixed positions).

Conduct when molten or dissolved in water - ions are free to move.
cards.newFront: State and explain the properties of ionic compounds (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• High melting/boiling points — strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions need lots of energy to overcome
  • Do not conduct when solid — ions are in fixed positions
  • Conduct when molten or aqueous — ions are free to move and carry charge

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
How are ionic compounds
formed?
cards.oldBack:
Reaction of a metal with a non-metal.
Electron transfer occurs - metal gives away its outer shell electrons to
non-metal.
cards.newFront:
How are ionic compounds
formed?
cards.newBack:
Reaction of a metal with a non-metal.
Electron transfer occurs - metal gives away its outer shell electrons to
non-metal.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
What are giant covalent
substances? Give properties and examples
cards.oldBack:
Solids, atoms covalently bonded together in a giant lattice.

High melting/boiling points – strong covalent bonds.

Mostly don’t conduct electricity (no delocalised e−)

Diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide (silica).
cards.newFront: Describe giant covalent structures: properties & examples (4 points)
cards.newBack:
• Billions of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds in a giant lattice
  • Very high melting/boiling points (many strong covalent bonds to break)
  • Usually do not conduct electricity (no delocalised electrons — except graphite)
  • Examples: diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide (SiO2)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Describe the structure and properties of diamond
cards.oldBack:
– four, strong covalent bonds for each carbon atom
– very hard (Strong bonds)
– very high melting point (strong bonds)
– does not conduct electricity (no delocalised electrons)
cards.newFront: Describe the structure and properties of diamond (4 points)
cards.newBack:
• Each carbon forms 4 strong covalent bonds (tetrahedral giant lattice)
  • Very hard and very high melting point (many strong covalent bonds)
  • Does not conduct electricity (no delocalised electrons)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: What is graphite? Explain its properties.
cards.oldBack:
– Giant covalent structure with three covalent bonds for each carbon atom forming layers of hexagonal rings
– layers free to slide as weak intermolecular forces between layers; soft, can be used as a lubricant
– high melting point
– conduct thermal and electricity due to one delocalised electron per each carbon atom
cards.newFront: Describe the structure and properties of graphite (4 points)
cards.newBack:
• Each carbon forms 3 strong covalent bonds in layers of hexagonal rings
  • Soft / slippery — weak intermolecular forces between layers let layers slide
  • High melting point — strong covalent bonds within layers
  • Conducts electricity — 1 delocalised electron per carbon is free to move

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Why is it often not possible to obtain the theoretical yield in a chemical reaction?
cards.oldBack:
Reversibility: The reaction may not go to completion because it is reversible, leading to an equilibrium where both reactants and products are present.

Product Loss: Some of the product may be lost during the process of separation from the reaction mixture

Side Reactions: Some of the reactants might undergo side reactions, producing unintended by-products.
cards.newFront: Give 3 reasons why actual yield is often less than theoretical yield
cards.newBack:
• Reversible reaction — may not go to completion
  • Product loss — during transfer, filtration or purification
  • Side reactions — reactants form unwanted by-products

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: How do Group 1 elements react with water? Describe the products.
cards.oldBack:
They react vigorously with water, fizzing and moving around on the surface.

Products: hydrogen gas is released and hydroxides are formed which dissolve to make an alkaline solution
cards.newFront: How do Group 1 metals react with water, and what are the products?
cards.newBack:
• React vigorously: fizz, float and move on the surface (potassium burns with a lilac flame)
  • Produce hydrogen gas and a metal hydroxide (dissolves to form an alkaline solution)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: State the first five halogens and their states of matter and colour (at room temperature)
cards.oldBack:
- Fluorine, pale yellow gas.
- Chlorine, pale green gas.
- Bromine, dark brown liquid (orange vapour and solution).
- Iodine, grey solid (gives off purple vapour when heated).

- Astatine, solid
cards.newFront: State the colour and state at room temperature of the halogens (Group 7)
cards.newBack:
• Fluorine: pale yellow gas · Chlorine: pale green gas
  • Bromine: red-brown liquid (orange vapour)
  • Iodine: grey solid (purple vapour when heated) · Astatine: black solid

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Explain the difference in how strong and weak acids behave when dissolved in water (aqueous solution)
cards.oldBack:
Strong acid is completely ionised in aqueous solution - it dissociates fully into its ions

Weak acid is only partially ionised - only a fraction of the acid molecules dissociate into ions
cards.newFront: Compare strong acids and weak acids in aqueous solution
cards.newBack:
• Strong acid: completely ionises (dissociates) in water → higher H+ concentration, lower pH
  • Weak acid: only partially ionises in water → lower H+ concentration, higher pH

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: What is the difference between a concentrated acid and a dilute acid, and how does this compare to strong and weak acids?
cards.oldBack:
A concentrated acid has more moles of acid per unit volume of water, while a dilute acid has fewer.

This differs from acid strength: a strong acid, which fully ionizes in water, typically has a lower pH, whereas a weak acid, which only partially ionizes, has a higher pH at the same concentration.
cards.newFront: Compare concentrated vs dilute acids with strong vs weak acids
cards.newBack:
• Concentrated vs dilute: how many moles of acid are dissolved per unit volume of water
  • Strong vs weak: whether the acid fully or partially ionises in water (at the same concentration, strong acids have lower pH)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
Describe the tests for
hydrogen, oxygen, carbon
dioxide and chlorine
cards.oldBack:
Hydrogen – ‘pop’ heard when burning splint placed over the gas.

Oxygen – glowing splint relights.

Carbon dioxide – turns limewater (Ca(OH)2) milky.

Chlorine – bleaches damp litmus paper white.
cards.newFront: State the tests for H<sub>2</sub>, O<sub>2</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub> and Cl<sub>2</sub> (4 gases)
cards.newBack:

  • Oxygen: relights a glowing splint
  • Carbon dioxide: turns limewater milky/cloudy

cards.subject: chemistry

cards.oldBack:
Add a solution containing barium ions - Ba2+ (E.g. BaCl2 solution). If sulfate anions are present, a white precipitate of BaSO4 forms

cards.newFront: Describe the test for sulfate ions (SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>)
cards.newBack:
• Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride (BaCl2) solution
  • Positive result: white precipitate of barium sulfate (BaSO4)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
Name four potential effects
of global climate change
cards.oldBack:
Any of these:
- Global warming
- Melting of glaciers and polar ice caps; sea level rise, flooding and increased coastal erosion.
- Changes in the amount, timing and distribution of rainfall and storms.
- Temperature and water stress for humans and wildlife.
- Changes in the food-producing capacity of some regions.
- Changes to the distribution of wildlife species.
cards.newFront: Give 4 potential effects of global climate change
cards.newBack:
• Melting glaciers & ice caps → rising sea levels and coastal flooding
  • More extreme weather & changed rainfall patterns
  • Habitat loss and shifts in wildlife distribution
  • Reduced crop yields / water stress in some regions

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: What are two issues regarding sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen?
cards.oldBack:
They cause respiratory problems in humans and cause acid rain.

Acid rain kills animals (by making the lakes in which they live in acidic) and damages plants and buildings.
cards.newFront: Give 2 problems caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
cards.newBack:
• Dissolve in rainwater to form acid rain (acidifies lakes, damages plants & limestone buildings)
  • Cause respiratory problems in humans

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Describe how to measure the rate of reaction by monitoring mass loss.
cards.oldBack:
Place the reaction flask on a balance. In these reactions (e.g. metal carbonate +
acid) a gas is given off, so record the decrease in mass in time intervals (note
hydrogen is too light). Plot a graph of mass vs time.
cards.newFront: How do you measure reaction rate by mass loss? (3 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Place the reaction flask (with cotton wool plug) on a mass balance
  • Record the decrease in mass at regular time intervals as gas escapes (not suitable for H2 — too light)
  • Plot mass against time; steeper gradient = faster rate

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
Describe how to measure the rate of reaction by monitoring the disappearance
of a cross.
cards.oldBack:
Take a piece of paper and mark a cross (X) on it. Put the reaction flask on this
cross. Mix the reagents, and measure how long it takes for a cloudy mixture to
conceal a cross.
cards.newFront: How do you measure reaction rate using the disappearing cross method?
cards.newBack:
• Place the reaction flask over a paper marked with a black cross (X)
  • Mix reactants and start a stopwatch
  • Measure the time taken for the precipitate/cloudiness to obscure the cross (rate ∝ 1 ÷ time)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: How do you determine the rate of reaction at a specific time t from a graph of reactant amount versus time?
cards.oldBack:
Draw a tangent to the curve at the point t. The slope of the tangent line represents the rate of reaction at time t.

A steeper tangent line indicates a faster rate.
cards.newFront: How do you find the rate of reaction at a specific time t from a graph?
cards.newBack:
• Draw a tangent to the curve at time t
  • Calculate the gradient (slope) of the tangent (steeper tangent = faster rate)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
Describe and explain the effect of increasing surface
area on a reaction
cards.oldBack:
Increasing the surface area of solid reactants (by e.g. cutting into smaller pieces) increases the frequency of
collisions and so increases the rate of reaction

e.g. block of magnesium reacts slower with acid then magnesium powder
cards.newFront: Explain the effect of increasing surface area on reaction rate
cards.newBack:
• Breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more surface particles
  • Increases the frequency of successful collisions → faster rate
  • Example: magnesium powder reacts faster with acid than a magnesium block

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Describe the effect of changing the concentration of reactant and product on the position of the equilibrium in a reversible reaction
cards.oldBack:
The system is no longer at equilibrium and the concentrations of all the substances will change until equilibrium is reached again.

- If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again.

- If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again.
cards.newFront: How does changing reactant or product concentration shift a reversible equilibrium?
cards.newBack:
• Increase reactant concentration: equilibrium shifts right → more product formed
  • Decrease product concentration: equilibrium shifts right → more reactants react to replace it

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront:
What is the empirical
formula? How is it related to
molecular formula?
cards.oldBack:
Simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of different elements in the compound.
The two are related by some numerical constant.
E.g. the empirical formula for heptene, C7H14, is CH2 . Multiplying the empirical formula by a numerical constant (7) would yield the molecular formula of heptene.
cards.newFront: What is the empirical formula and how does it relate to the molecular formula?
cards.newBack:
• Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound
  • Molecular formula = empirical formula × a whole-number multiplier (e.g. CH2 × 7 → C7H14)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Describe the physical properties of alkanes (including the trend with bigger molecules)
cards.oldBack:
- Poor reactivity.
- Boiling points and viscosity increase as molecules get bigger (smallest molecules are gases, then liquids and biggest are solids.)
- Volatility and flammability decrease as molecules get bigger.
cards.newFront: Describe the physical properties and trends of alkanes as chain length increases (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Boiling point and viscosity increase (stronger intermolecular forces)
  • Volatility and flammability decrease
  • Generally unreactive (saturated — only single C–C bonds)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: What is the first step in the fractional distillation of crude oil?
cards.oldBack: Crude oil is heated and vaporized, and the vapor rises up the fractionating column, which is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top.
cards.newFront: What is the first step in the fractional distillation of crude oil?
cards.newBack: Crude oil is heated and vaporised, and the vapour rises up the fractionating column, which is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Compare the combustion of alkanes and alkenes
cards.oldBack:
Alkanes: Burn with a cleaner flame, producing less soot and primarily forming carbon dioxide and water.

Alkenes: Burn with a smokier flame, often producing more soot due to a lower hydrogen-to-carbon ratio and the presence of double bonds.
cards.newFront: Compare the combustion of alkanes and alkenes
cards.newBack:
• Alkanes: burn with a cleaner flame (less soot; mostly CO2 + H2O)
  • Alkenes: burn with a smokier flame (more incomplete combustion / soot due to a higher C:H ratio)

cards.oldFront: Explain what happens to the double bond when alkanes are used to produce polymers?
cards.oldBack: The C=C double bond becomes just a single bond, and the the two carbons make other bonds.
cards.newFront: Explain what happens to the double bond when alkenes are used to produce polymers?
cards.newBack: The C=C double bond becomes a single bond, and the two carbons form bonds to neighbouring monomers.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: How do alkanes undergo halogenation, and what conditions are necessary for this reaction to occur?
cards.oldBack:
The reaction replaces hydrogen atoms with halogen atoms.

UV light is needed to break halogen molecules into free atoms (e.g. Cl2 becomes 2Cl).

cards.oldBack:
Qualitative test used to identify metal ions (cations).

Carried out by inserting a nichrome wire loop with the unknown compound on into a flame and observing the colour.
cards.newFront: How do you carry out a flame test? (3 steps)
