cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Describe sacrificial protection
cards.oldBack: The protection of a metal (e.g. iron) against corrosion by coating with a more reactive metal (e.g zinc). This creates a physical barrier to oxygen and water, preventing corrosion
cards.newFront: Explain how sacrificial protection prevents iron from rusting (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Attach or coat iron with a more reactive metal (e.g. zinc or magnesium)
  • The more reactive metal loses electrons (oxidises) more easily than iron
  • It corrodes instead of the iron — even if the coating is scratched

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Describe evaporation/crystallisation (as a separation method)
cards.oldBack:
Evaporation/crystallisation separates dissolved soluble solids from solutions (e.g., salt from water).

Heat the solution until crystals start to form, leave the solution to cool and then filter the formed crystals from the solution as the solvent evaporates.
cards.newFront: Describe crystallisation (3 steps)
cards.newBack:
Separates a soluble solid from a solution:
  • Heat gently to evaporate some water until a saturated solution forms (crystals appear at the edge)
  • Leave to cool so crystals form
  • Filter off the crystals and pat dry with filter paper

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Define gas
cards.oldBack: The state of matter where the particles have the most energy. The particles in a gas are relatively spread out and move randomly in all directions. Intermolecular forces acting between the particles are very weak.
cards.newFront: Describe the arrangement, movement and energy of particles in a gas (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Far apart and randomly arranged
  • Move rapidly and randomly in all directions
  • Highest kinetic energy; very weak forces between particles

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Define liquid
cards.oldBack:
The state of matter where the particles are arranged randomly and close together.
The particles are able to move past each other. Intermolecular forces act between the particles.
cards.newFront: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in a liquid (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Close together in a random/irregular arrangement
  • Can slide / move past each other
  • Moderate forces of attraction between particles

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Define percentage yield
cards.oldBack: The percentage ratio of the actual yield of product from a reaction compared with the theoretical yield.
cards.newFront: Define percentage yield
cards.newBack:
Ratio of actual product obtained to the theoretical maximum, as a percentage:
Percentage yield = actual yieldtheoretical yield × 100

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Describe simple distillation
cards.oldBack:
A separation technique used to separate a liquid from a solution.

The solution is heated so that only the liquid with the lowest boiling point evaporates. This gas is then condensed in a condenser before being collected as a liquid.
cards.newFront: Describe simple distillation (3 points)
cards.newBack:
Separates a pure liquid (solvent) from a solution:
  • Heat the solution so the solvent evaporates / boils
  • Vapour passes into a cold condenser and condenses back into liquid
  • Pure liquid is collected as the distillate

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Define solid
cards.oldBack:
The state of matter where the particles hold a regular arrangement and have the least
amount of energy. They are tightly packed together and can only vibrate about their fixed positions. Strong intermolecular forces act between the particles
cards.newFront: Describe the arrangement, movement and energy of particles in a solid (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Regular arrangement, tightly packed together
  • Vibrate about fixed positions only
  • Least kinetic energy; strong forces between particles

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Define effect of surface area on reaction rate
cards.oldBack:
Increasing the surface area of the reactants means
there are more exposed reacting particles. This means there are more frequent successful
collisions, so the rate of reaction increases.
cards.newFront: Explain in terms of collisions why increasing surface area increases reaction rate
cards.newBack:
• More reacting particles are exposed at the surface
  • More frequent successful collisions → higher rate of reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Define effect of temperature on reaction rate
cards.oldBack:
Increasing the temperature means the particles will
have more kinetic energy and so will move faster. If the molecules are moving faster they will
collide more often and, since they’ve gained kinetic energy, a larger proportion of the
particles will have at least the activation energy. For both these reasons the rate of reaction
increases.
cards.newFront: Explain in terms of collisions why increasing temperature increases reaction rate (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Particles have more kinetic energy and move faster → more frequent collisions
  • A greater proportion of particles have energy ≥ the activation energy
  • Many more frequent successful collisions → faster rate

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Define molar enthalpy change
cards.oldBack:
The amount of heat energy given out or absorbed by one mole of a
substance during a reaction. It can be calculated from heat energy change, Q, by dividing Q
by the amount of moles of the substance which took part in the reaction. The value is made
negative if the reaction was exothermic.
cards.newFront: Define molar enthalpy change (ΔH) and how to calculate it (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Heat energy released or absorbed per 1 mole of substance reacted
  • Formula: ΔH = Q ÷ moles (in kJ/mol)
  • Sign: negative (−) for exothermic, positive (+) for endothermic

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Define crude oil
cards.oldBack:
A finite resource found in rocks. It is the remains of an ancient biomass consisting
mainly of plankton that was buried in mud. Most of the compounds in crude oil are
hydrocarbons.
cards.newFront: What is crude oil? (3 points)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: Define general formula

the composition of the atoms present in the compound. For example, alkanes have the
general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, where n is the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.

  • Example: alkanes = CnH2n+2 (where n = number of carbon atoms)

cards.oldBack: A substance is soluble if it can be dissolved in a solvent, e.g. salt in water. An insoluble substance won’t dissolve in a particular solvent.
cards.newFront: What does soluble mean?
cards.newBack: A substance is soluble if it can be dissolved in a solvent, e.g. salt in water. An insoluble substance won’t dissolve in a particular solvent.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.oldFront: What is the link between relative formula mass and moles
cards.oldBack: Relative formula mass of a substance is numerically equal to the mass of one mole of the substance in grams
cards.newFront: What is the link between relative formula mass and moles
cards.newBack: Relative formula mass of a substance is numerically equal to the mass of one mole of the substance in grams

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: What information can you read from a paper chromatogram? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• 1 spot = pure substance; 2 or more spots = mixture
  • Spots at the same height (same Rf value) indicate the same substance
  • A spot that stays on the baseline is insoluble in that solvent

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Core practical: give 3 key precautions when setting up paper chromatography
cards.newBack:
• Draw the baseline in pencil (graphite is insoluble so it won’t run up the paper)
  • Keep the solvent level below the pencil line so spots don’t dissolve directly into the solvent
  • Cover the beaker with a lid to prevent volatile solvent evaporating; mark the solvent front before drying

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: State the formula linking moles, mass and relative formula mass (Mr)
cards.newBack:
moles = mass (g)Mr (or Ar)
  • Rearranged: mass = moles × Mr
  • Mr = sum of the relative atomic masses (Ar) of all atoms in the formula

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: What are the 3 steps to calculate a reacting mass from a balanced equation?
cards.newBack:
• Step 1: find moles of the known substance (moles = mass ÷ Mr)
  • Step 2: use the molar ratio from the balanced equation to find moles of the unknown
  • Step 3: convert back to mass (mass = moles × Mr)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: How do you calculate empirical formula and then molecular formula from data? (3 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Step 1: divide the mass (or %) of each element by its Ar to get moles
  • Step 2: divide every mole value by the smallest → simplest whole-number ratio (empirical formula)
  • Step 3: multiplier = Mr ÷ empirical formula mass; multiply empirical subscripts by this number

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you determine the formula of magnesium oxide by combustion? (4 points)
cards.newBack:
• Weigh crucible + lid, add coiled magnesium and reweigh
  • Heat strongly, lifting the lid briefly to let O2 in without letting white MgO smoke escape
  • Heat to constant mass so all Mg has completely reacted
  • Mass of O = mass of MgO − mass of Mg → convert both masses to moles (÷ Ar) for the ratio

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: How do you write the formula of an ionic compound from its ions?
cards.newBack:
• Balance the ion numbers so total positive charge = total negative charge (overall neutral)
  • Use brackets if you need more than one compound ion (e.g. Mg2+ + 2 OH− → Mg(OH)2; 2 NH4+ + SO42− → (NH4)2SO4)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: What are the 3 rules for drawing an ionic dot-and-cross diagram?
cards.newBack:
• Show outer-shell electrons using dots for one element and crosses for the other
  • Metal atom loses outer electrons; non-metal gains them to achieve a full outer shell
  • Put square brackets around each ion with its charge outside top-right (e.g. [Mg]2+)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Define a covalent bond in terms of electrostatic attraction
cards.newBack: • A strong electrostatic attraction between the positively charged nuclei of two non-metal atoms and the shared pair(s) of negatively charged electrons between them

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: How many covalent bonds do H, halogens, O, N and C normally form in dot-and-cross diagrams?
cards.newBack:
• H & halogens (Group 7): 1 bond (e.g. H2, HCl, Cl2)
  • Oxygen: 2 bonds (H2O has 2 singles; O2 has 1 double bond)
  • Nitrogen: 3 bonds (NH3 has 3 singles; N2 has 1 triple bond)
  • Carbon: 4 bonds (CH4 4 singles; CO2 two double bonds; C2H4 one C=C double bond)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Why do covalent compounds not usually conduct electricity?
cards.newBack:
• Covalent molecules are electrically neutral (no overall charge)
  • They have no free-moving ions and no delocalised electrons to carry charge (exception: graphite)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: How do reactions of Li, Na and K with water show the Group 1 reactivity trend? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Reactivity increases down Group 1 (Li < Na < K)
  • Evidence: Li fizzes steadily; Na melts into a ball and fizzes faster; K ignites immediately with a lilac flame
  • Outer electron is further from the nucleus (more shells/shielding) → weaker attraction → lost more easily

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: How do colour, melting/boiling point and reactivity change going down Group 7 (halogens)?
cards.newBack:
Going down Group 7 (F → Cl → Br → I → At):
  • Colour gets darker (pale yellow → pale green → red-brown → grey → black)
  • Melting & boiling points increase (gas → liquid → solid)
  • Reactivity decreases (outer shell further from nucleus → harder to gain an electron)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: How do iron or phosphorus experiments determine the percentage of oxygen in air?
cards.newBack:
• Wet iron filings (rusting) or heated phosphorus reacts with all the O2 in a trapped volume of air
  • The gas volume decreases by about 21% (water rises up the tube)
  • % O2 = (decrease in volume ÷ initial volume of air) × 100

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Core practical: give 3 precautions when finding the % of oxygen in air
cards.newBack:
• Use an excess of iron/copper/phosphorus so all the oxygen reacts
  • Ensure the apparatus is completely airtight
  • Allow the apparatus to cool back to room temperature before measuring the final gas volume

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: State the Reactivity Series of metals from most reactive to least reactive
cards.newBack: Potassium > Sodium > Lithium > Calcium > Magnesium > Aluminium > (Carbon) > Zinc > Iron > (Hydrogen) > Copper > Silver > Gold

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you compare the reactivity of Mg, Zn, Fe and Cu with dilute acid?
cards.newBack:
• Add equal masses/surface areas of each metal to equal volumes & concentrations of dilute HCl or H2SO4
  • Compare rate of fizzing (H2) and temperature rise
  • Order: Mg (vigorous) > Zn (steady) > Fe (slow) > Cu (no reaction)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Define an acid and a base in terms of proton transfer
cards.newBack:
• Acid: a proton (H+) donor
  • Base: a proton (H+) acceptor

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: What types of substance act as bases, and how is an alkali different?
cards.newBack:
• Bases: substances that neutralise acids — metal oxides, metal hydroxides, and ammonia
  • Alkalis: soluble bases that dissolve in water to produce OH− ions

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Describe how to prepare a pure, dry soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble base (4 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Warm the dilute acid and add excess insoluble base (until solid remains, ensuring all acid reacts)
  • Filter to remove the excess unreacted solid
  • Heat gently to evaporate some water until saturated (crystals start forming)
  • Leave to cool to crystallise, filter off crystals, and pat dry with filter paper

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you make pure, dry hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals?
cards.newBack:
• Warm dilute sulfuric acid (H2SO4) and add excess black copper(II) oxide (CuO) while stirring
  • Filter out excess black CuO to obtain a clear blue CuSO4 solution
  • Evaporate some water over a water bath/gentle flame, then cool to form blue crystals
  • Filter off crystals and pat dry between filter papers

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: What is the physical test to show a sample of water is pure?
cards.newBack:
• Measure its boiling point (pure water boils sharply at 100 °C) or melting/freezing point (0 °C)
  • Impurities raise the boiling point and lower the freezing point

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: State the equation for heat energy change (Q) and define every symbol
cards.newBack:
Q = m c ΔT
  • Q = heat energy transferred (J)
  • m = mass of water/solution heated (g; 1 cm3 = 1 g)
  • c = specific heat capacity of water (4.18 J/(g °C))
  • ΔT = temperature change (°C)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you reduce errors when measuring temperature changes (calorimetry)? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Solutions (dissolving/neutralisation/displacement): use an insulated polystyrene cup + lid inside a beaker and stir continuously
  • Combustion (spirit burner): use a draught shield and stir the water in a copper can
  • Main source of error: heat loss to the surroundings (and incomplete combustion)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you investigate different solid catalysts on H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> decomposition? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Add equal masses of different solids (e.g. MnO2, CuO) to equal volumes/concentrations of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)
  • Measure the volume of O2 collected in a gas syringe in a fixed time (fastest = best catalyst)
  • Filter, dry and reweigh the solid to confirm its mass is unchanged

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Describe the 2 specification examples of reversible reactions
cards.newBack:
• Hydrated copper(II) sulfate (blue) ⇌ anhydrous CuSO4 (white) + water (heat → white; add water → blue + gets hot)
  • Ammonium chloride (white solid) ⇌ ammonia (NH3) + hydrogen chloride (HCl) (heat decomposes; cooling reforms white solid)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: State the IUPAC prefixes for 1–6 carbons and endings for alkanes & alkenes
cards.newBack:
• 1 C: meth- · 2 C: eth- · 3 C: prop- · 4 C: but- · 5 C: pent- · 6 C: hex-
  • -ane: alkane (single bonds) · -ene: alkene (C=C double bond; number gives lowest position, e.g. but-1-ene)
  • Halogens use prefixes: chloro-, bromo- (e.g. 1,2-dibromoethane)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Distinguish between molecular, structural and displayed formulae (plus isomers)
cards.newBack:
• Molecular: actual numbers of each atom (e.g. C4H10)
  • Structural: atoms grouped carbon-by-carbon (e.g. CH3CH2CH2CH3)
  • Displayed: draws every atom and every covalent bond
  • Isomers: same molecular formula, different structural formula

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Why is carbon monoxide (CO) poisonous? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• CO binds strongly (irreversibly) to haemoglobin in red blood cells
  • Reduces the blood’s capacity to carry oxygen around the body (can cause suffocation/death)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: How are oxides of nitrogen formed in car engines?
cards.newBack:
• Very high temperatures inside car engines provide enough energy for nitrogen and oxygen from the air to react together
  • Forms oxides of nitrogen (NOx), which contribute to acid rain

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Why is cracking necessary in the oil industry? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Crude oil has a surplus of long-chain hydrocarbons (low demand, thick/viscous) and a shortage of short-chain alkanes (high demand for petrol/fuels)
  • Cracking also produces alkenes, needed as raw materials for making polymers

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: What is the functional group of alkenes?
cards.newBack:
• A carbon–carbon double covalent bond (>C=C<)
  • Makes alkenes unsaturated and more reactive than alkanes

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Name the alkenes with 2, 3 and 4 carbons (including the two unbranched butene isomers)
cards.newBack:
• 2 C: ethene (CH2=CH2)
  • 3 C: propene (CH2=CHCH3)
  • 4 C (unbranched isomers): but-1-ene (CH2=CHCH2CH3) and but-2-ene (CH3CH=CHCH3)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: How do you convert between an alkene monomer and its addition polymer repeat unit?
cards.newBack:
• Monomer → repeat unit: change C=C to a C–C single bond, draw two trailing bonds extending through brackets, add subscript n
  • Repeat unit → monomer: remove brackets & trailing bonds and restore the C=C double bond

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you investigate surface area and acid concentration using marble chips and dilute HCl? (4 points)
cards.newBack:
• React calcium carbonate (marble chips) + dilute HCl → CO2 gas
  • Measure rate by volume of CO2 (gas syringe / upturned cylinder) or mass loss on a balance at regular time intervals
  • Surface area: compare equal masses of large vs small marble chips (same acid volume, concentration & temperature)
  • Concentration: vary HCl concentration (same mass/size of marble chips & temperature) → smaller chips / higher concentration give steeper initial gradient

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: On a chromatogram, how can you tell if an unknown dye contains a specific reference colouring?
cards.newBack:
• Run both samples on the same chromatogram in the same solvent
  • If the unknown produces a spot at the exact same height (same Rf value) as the reference, that substance is present

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: In paper chromatography, why must the baseline be drawn in pencil and kept above the solvent level?
cards.newBack:
• Pencil (graphite): insoluble in the solvent, so it won’t dissolve and smudge/run up the paper like ink would
  • Above solvent level: stops the sample spots dissolving straight into the solvent at the bottom

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Write the chemical formulae for: magnesium chloride, aluminium oxide, and calcium hydroxide
cards.newBack:
• Magnesium chloride (Mg2+, Cl−): MgCl2
  • Aluminium oxide (Al3+, O2−): Al2O3
  • Calcium hydroxide (Ca2+, OH−): Ca(OH)2

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Write the balanced symbol equation for sodium reacting with water
cards.newBack:
2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g)
(Same pattern for Li and K: forms alkaline metal hydroxide + hydrogen gas)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Predict the state, colour and reactivity of astatine (bottom of Group 7)
cards.newBack:
• State & colour: dark black solid at room temperature (highest melting/boiling point in Group 7)
  • Reactivity: least reactive halogen (outer shell furthest from nucleus, hardest to gain an electron)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: In the copper / iron % oxygen in air experiment, why might your measured value come out less than 21%?
cards.newBack:
• Not enough metal (not in excess) or not heated/left long enough → not all O2 reacted
  • Apparatus was not cooled back to room temperature before reading final gas volume (warm gas expands)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: Which metals in the Reactivity Series do not react with dilute acids, and why?
cards.newBack:
• Copper, silver and gold
  • They are below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so they cannot displace H+ ions from acids

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: In Q = mcΔT, what mistake do students make with m when a small mass of solid dissolves in 50 cm3 of water?
cards.newBack:
• m is the mass of water/solution heated (50 g), not the mass of the solid added
  • For aqueous solutions assume 1 cm3 = 1 g and c = 4.18 J/(g °C)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: How is carbon monoxide (CO) formed from hydrocarbon fuels?
cards.newBack:
• Formed by incomplete combustion when a hydrocarbon burns in a limited supply of oxygen
  • Also produces soot (carbon) and water

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.newFront: What is the chemical test to distinguish an alkene from an alkane?
cards.newBack:
• Shake with orange bromine water
  • Alkene (C=C): decolourises bromine water (orange → colourless)
  • Alkane: stays orange (no reaction in the dark)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define Newton's first law
cards.oldBack: If a stationary object’s resultant force is zero, the object will remain stationary. If a moving object’s resultant force is zero, the object will continue to move at a constant velocity (same speed and direction).
cards.newFront: State Newton's first law (2 cases)
cards.newBack:
When the resultant force is zero:
  • A stationary object stays stationary
  • A moving object continues at constant velocity (same speed and direction)

What is meant by acceleration?
Give its unit.

  • B: constant acceleration (sloping upward)
  • C: constant deceleration (sloping downward)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Explain what is the difference between elastic and plastic behavior.
cards.oldBack:
In elastic behaviour, object recovers its original shape when the forces causing the extension is removed.

In plastic behavior, there is a permanent deformation to the shape of the object when forces are removed.
cards.newFront: Compare elastic and plastic behaviour
cards.newBack:
• Elastic behaviour: object returns to its original shape when the force is removed
  • Plastic behaviour: object is permanently deformed when the force is removed

cards.oldFront: Define earth wire (incl. colour)
cards.oldBack: The green and yellow wire connected to metal casings of appliances, that prevents an appliance from becoming live.

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: What is a fuse and where is it placed?
cards.oldBack:
A safety device consisting of a thin metal filament that melts and cuts off the power
supply if there is a surge in current grater than its rating value, e.g. 5A. Fuses are connected to the live wire.
cards.newFront: What is a fuse, how does it work, and which wire is it on?
cards.newBack:
• Safety device containing a thin metal wire
  • If current exceeds its rating (e.g. 5 A), the wire melts and breaks the circuit
  • Always connected in the live wire

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define light emitting diode (LED)
cards.oldBack:
A device that gives out light when a current flows through it. Current
can only flow through it in one direction, and a minimum voltage must be applied across it
before it illuminates.
cards.newFront: Describe a light-emitting diode (LED) (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Allows current to flow in one direction only
  • Emits light when current flows through it
  • Requires a minimum voltage before it lights up (useful for indicating current)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define parallel circuit
cards.oldBack: Components connected in parallel have the same potential difference (voltage) across each component. The total current is equal to the sum of the currents flowing through each component.
cards.newFront: State the rules for voltage and current in a parallel circuit
cards.newBack:
• Voltage (p.d.): the same across every branch
  • Current: total current = sum of currents in each branch

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define volt
cards.oldBack: The unit of potential difference (voltage). One volt is equal to one joule per coulomb.
cards.newFront: Define volt

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Describe the structure of the atom, including particle names and charges.
cards.oldBack: The atom has a positively charged nucleus which is made up of protons (+1) and neutrons (0). The nucleus is surrounded by electrons (-1), which all orbit the nucleus at different distances.
cards.newFront: Describe the structure of an atom, including particle charges
cards.newBack:
• Small, dense, positively charged nucleus containing protons (+1) and neutrons (0)
  • Surrounded by electrons (−1) orbiting in shells at different distances

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What are the differences between series
and parallel circuits in regards to current
and voltage?
cards.oldBack:
In series:
- The same current flows through all the components
- The potential difference across the components is not the same. The total potential difference is equal to the sum of potential differences across each component.

In parallel:
- The sum of the currents in each section is equal to the total current.

- The potential difference across each branch is the same.
cards.newFront: Compare current and voltage in series vs parallel circuits
cards.newBack:
• Series: current is the same everywhere; total voltage = sum of component voltages
  • Parallel: voltage is the same across each branch; total current = sum of branch currents

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: What is an voltmeter and where must it be connected in a circuit?
cards.oldBack: A device that is connected in parallel with a component to measure the potential difference (voltage) across it.
cards.newFront: What is a voltmeter and where must it be connected in a circuit?
cards.newBack: A device that is connected in parallel with a component to measure the potential difference (voltage) across it.

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
How does changing the resistance in a
circuit change the current?
cards.oldBack:
● Current is inversely proportional to resistance. Therefore at a constant voltage, increasing the resistance will decrease the current.

● In an electrical circuit the flow of electrons causes a current. A high resistance makes it harder for electrons to pass through and therefore reduces the current.
cards.newFront: How does changing resistance affect current (at constant voltage)? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Current is inversely proportional to resistance — higher resistance gives a smaller current
  • Higher resistance makes it harder for electrons to flow through the circuit

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
Explain the relationship between voltage,
current and resistance in a filament
lamp.
cards.oldBack:
As temperature increases in the lamp, the resistance also increases. This is because a higher temperature makes the atoms in the filament vibrate more, making it harder for electrons to pass through. This therefore decreases the current.

A filament lamp is not ohmic, meaning that current is not directly proportional to the potential difference. If voltage is double, current will not be doubled since there will be an increase in resistance
cards.newFront: Explain the I–V relationship for a filament lamp (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• As current rises, the filament gets hotter
  • Metal ions vibrate more → more frequent electron collisions → resistance increases
  • Non-ohmic: current is not directly proportional to voltage (I–V graph curves and flattens)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
When an electrical current flows through
a resistor why does it heat up?
cards.oldBack:
There are collisions between the electrons and
the ions in the resistor’s lattice. This causes a
transfer of kinetic energy into thermal energy,
which is released into the surroundings.
cards.newFront: Why does a resistor heat up when current flows through it? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Flowing electrons collide with metal ions in the resistor’s lattice
  • Energy is transferred from electrical/kinetic energy to thermal energy in the surroundings

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What are some advantages and
disadvantages of the heating effect?
cards.oldBack:
Advantages:
- Can be used for appliances such as toasters or electrical fires, where the hot wire helps heat the bread or room

Disadvantages:
- The loss of energy as heat energy can make an appliance inefficient
- If an appliance overheats it can catch fire or overheat, which could ruin the device or injure the user
cards.newFront: Give 1 advantage and 2 disadvantages of the electrical heating effect
cards.newBack:
• Advantage: useful in heating appliances (kettles, toasters, electric heaters)
  • Disadvantages: wastes energy (lowers efficiency); overheating can damage components or cause fire

cards.newFront: Which voltage–time graph shows a.c. and which shows d.c.?
cards.newBack:
• A: alternating current (a.c.) — continuously reverses direction
  • B: direct current (d.c.) — flows in one direction only

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: How does an earth wire ensure safety?
cards.oldBack:
The earth wire is connected to the metal casing
of the device and provides a low resistance path
to the ground. Therefore if a fault occurs the
earth wire allows the large currents in the live
wire to flow through to the ground.
cards.newFront: How does an earth wire keep a metal-cased appliance safe? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Connected to the metal casing, providing a low-resistance path to ground
  • If the live wire touches the casing, a large current flows to earth
  • This melts the fuse / trips the circuit breaker, cutting off the supply

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
Why is it important to connect a fuse or
switch to the live wire?
cards.oldBack:
When the switch is turned off, or when the fuse
breaks, it will break the circuit and stop current
running through the wire since live wire carries
the voltage. This provides a method to stop
current flowing into the appliance.
cards.newFront: Why must a fuse or switch be connected in the live wire? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• The live wire carries the high voltage (230 V) from the supply
  • Breaking the live wire isolates the appliance so it cannot remain live and cause an electric shock

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Which connection is not required when the appliance is double insulated? Give a reason for your answer.
cards.oldBack:
Earth wire is not required.
Because earth wire is connected to the casing of the material. If casing is made out of plastic(insulator), earth wire will not be able to let the current flow to the ground.
cards.newFront: Which wire is not needed in a double-insulated appliance, and why?
cards.newBack:
• Earth wire is not required
  • The outer casing is made of plastic (an electrical insulator), so it cannot become live

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Describe gamma rays, including uses and issues
cards.oldBack:
High energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from a nucleus.

Used for detecting and treating cancers, and sterilising food and medical implements.

Can cause cell damage and mutations.

They have a very high penetrating power and require several centimetre of lead to absorb them.
cards.newFront: Describe gamma rays: nature, penetration, uses and hazards (4 points)
cards.newBack:
• High-energy electromagnetic wave emitted from an unstable nucleus
  • Very high penetration — needs several centimetres of lead or thick concrete to absorb
  • Uses: sterilising food/medical kit, detecting & treating cancer
  • Hazard: ionising — can cause cell damage and DNA mutations

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define Hertz (Hz)
cards.oldBack: The unit of frequency.
cards.newFront: Define Hertz (Hz)
cards.newBack: The unit of frequency.

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define ray diagram
cards.oldBack:
A visual representation of the path of a wave, usually around the point where
it meets a boundary. Rays are usually drawn as straight lines with an arrow pointing in their
direction of travel.
cards.newFront: What is a ray diagram?
cards.newBack:
• A diagram showing the path of light / waves (e.g. at a mirror or glass boundary)
  • Drawn as straight lines with arrows showing the direction of wave travel

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
At what speed does an electromagnetic
wave travel in a vacuum?
cards.oldBack: 3 x10<sup>8</sup> m/s
cards.newFront:
At what speed does an electromagnetic
wave travel in a vacuum?
cards.newBack: 3 x10<sup>8</sup> m/s

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What are the four common properties of all
electromagnetic waves?
cards.oldBack:
· They are all transverse waves
· They all transfer energy or information
· They all travel at the speed of light in vacuum
· They all can be reflected, refracted or diffracted
cards.newFront: Give 4 properties shared by all electromagnetic waves
cards.newBack:
• All are transverse waves
  • All travel at the same speed in a vacuum (speed of light, 3 × 108 m/s)
  • All transfer energy (and information)
  • All can be reflected and refracted

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What happens when light is refracted
while passing through 2 different media?
cards.oldBack:
● The light changes speed and direction in the new medium
● If the new medium is more dense, the light will travel slower and bend towards the normal
● If the new medium is less dense, the light will travel faster and bend away from the normal
cards.newFront: What happens to light when it refracts at a boundary? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Light changes speed and (at an angle) direction
  • Entering a more optically dense medium: slows down and bends towards the normal
  • Entering a less optically dense medium: speeds up and bends away from the normal

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: What is the critical angle?
cards.oldBack: The angle of incidence which causes the angle of reflection to be 90 degrees so that that the light refracts onto the boundary.
cards.newFront: What is the critical angle?
cards.newBack: The angle of incidence in the denser medium that produces an angle of refraction of 90° (light refracts along the boundary).

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: What is total internal reflection?
cards.oldBack:
When light is trying to pass from a less dense
medium to a denser medium, it can be reflected
back to the less dense medium if the angle of
incidence is larger than the critical angle between
two media.
cards.newFront: What are the 2 conditions for total internal reflection (TIR)?
cards.newBack:
• Light must travel from a more optically dense medium towards a less optically dense medium (e.g. glass → air)
  • The angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle (i > c)
  • All the light is reflected back inside the denser medium

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: How does sonar work?
cards.oldBack:
When ultrasound waves are emitted they reflect off
boundaries and their echoes are detected. The speed of the
ultrasound is known and also the time it takes to detect the
echoes. The equation distance=speed x time is used to find
the distance between the ultrasound emitter and the
boundary (the distance calculated would be double the actual
distance as the sound has travelled there and back).
cards.newFront: How does sonar / echo-sounding measure distance? (3 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Emit a pulse of sound/ultrasound; it reflects off a boundary and the echo is detected
  • Measure total time t and calculate total distance = speed × time
  • Divide by 2 (because the wave travelled there and back)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Which letter represents wavelength
cards.oldBack: D
cards.newFront: Which letter represents the wavelength?
cards.newBack: D (distance from one crest to the next crest — one complete wave cycle)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Which letter represents amplitude
cards.oldBack: A
cards.newFront: Which letter represents the amplitude?
cards.newBack: A (maximum displacement from the central equilibrium rest position to a crest or trough)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define gravitational potential energy
cards.oldBack:
The store of energy that all raised matter has. It is directly
proportional to the mass of the object, the distance that it is raised, and the gravitational field
strength at that point.
cards.newFront: Define gravitational potential energy (GPE)
cards.newBack:
• Energy stored by an object because of its position in a gravitational field (height)
  • Depends on mass, gravitational field strength (g) and height (GPE = mgh)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define joule
cards.oldBack:
The unit used for energy. Equal to the work done when a force of one Newton acts
over a distance of one metre.
cards.newFront: Define joule
cards.newBack:
The unit used for energy. Equal to the work done when a force of one Newton acts
over a distance of one metre.

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define work done
cards.oldBack:
Work is done on an object when a force causes it to move through a distance. It
is equal to the product of the distance travelled and the magnitude of the force in the
direction of motion.
cards.newFront: Define work done
cards.newBack:
• Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance
  • Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force (W = Fd)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: What is wasted energy?
cards.oldBack:
● The energy that is not used by the device for its desired purpose is the waste energy.

● An example is a kettle: when energy is changed to sound energy it is classed as waste energy since it is not being used to heat the water.
cards.newFront: What is wasted energy? Give an example.
cards.newBack:
• Energy transferred to a store that is not useful for the device’s intended purpose (usually dissipated as thermal energy)
  • Example: sound or heat lost to the air from a kettle

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Explain why electrical heater of a kettle is placed at the bottom
cards.oldBack: Heat is mainly transferred by convection within fluids. When a part of the liquid is heated, it expands and becomes less dense therefore it rises up within the fluid. Colder part of the liquid is now denser so it sinks down within the liquid and this forms a convection current when heater is placed at the bottom.
cards.newFront: Explain why a kettle’s heating element is placed at the bottom (4 points)
cards.newBack:
• Water at the bottom is heated, expands and becomes less dense
  • Warm, less dense water rises
  • Cooler, denser water sinks to replace it
  • Sets up a convection current that heats all the water

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
How can you reduce unwanted heat
transfer?
cards.oldBack:
● Insulation in walls and ceilings, this causes the room to be heated up slower or cooled down slower

● Double glazed windows reduces conduction by putting air or vacuum in between

● Curtains to prevent heat loss by radiation etc.
cards.newFront: Give 3 ways to reduce unwanted heat transfer in a home
cards.newBack:
• Loft / cavity wall insulation — traps air to reduce conduction & convection
  • Double glazing — trapped air/vacuum gap reduces conduction
  • Curtains / shiny foil — reduce heat loss by convection and infrared radiation

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What is the relationship between work
done on an object and energy
transferred to the object?
cards.oldBack: Work Done = Energy Transferred
cards.newFront:
What is the relationship between work
done on an object and energy
transferred to the object?
cards.newBack:
Work done = energy transferred
W = ΔE

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: What is 1 Watt equivlanent to in terms of other units?
cards.oldBack: 1 Watt = 1 joule per second (J/s).
cards.newFront: What is 1 watt equivalent to in terms of other units?
cards.newBack: 1 Watt = 1 joule per second (J/s).

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define absolute zero
cards.oldBack:
The lowest possible temperature: −273°C or 0K. At this temperature the particles have no
kinetic energy and so are completely stationary.
cards.newFront: Define absolute zero
cards.newBack:
The lowest possible temperature: −273°C or 0K. At this temperature the particles have no
kinetic energy and so are completely stationary.

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define Pascals
cards.oldBack:
The unit of pressure, equal to a force of one Newton acting perpendicular to an
area of one metre squared.
cards.newFront: Define Pascals
cards.newBack:
The unit of pressure, equal to a force of one Newton acting perpendicular to an
area of one metre squared.

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define temperature
cards.oldBack:
A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. An
increase in temperature will result in an increase in the particles’ kinetic energies and
velocities.
cards.newFront: Define temperature in terms of particles
cards.newBack:
• A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance
  • Higher temperature → particles have higher average kinetic energy and move faster

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: How can Pascals be expressed in other units?
cards.newFront: How can Pascals be expressed in other units?
cards.newBack:
1 Pa = 1 Nm2
(1 newton per square metre)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
How do you convert between degree
Celsius and Kelvin?
cards.newFront:
How do you convert between degree
Celsius and Kelvin?
cards.newBack:
• °C → K: add 273 (T(K) = θ(°C) + 273)
  • K → °C: subtract 273 (θ(°C) = T(K) − 273)
  • Absolute zero: 0 K = −273 °C

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
Explain the pressure of a gas in terms of
the motion of particles.
cards.oldBack:
The particles move in random directions. When
they collide with the walls of a container they
exert a force which acts at a right angle to the
container. This causes pressure.
cards.newFront: Explain how a gas exerts pressure on its container walls (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Gas particles move rapidly in random directions
  • They collide with the container walls, exerting a force at right angles to the wall
  • Total force per unit area = pressure

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
How does temperature affect the
pressure of a gas?
cards.oldBack:
Increasing temperature increases the average
kinetic energy of particles so they move faster.
Therefore particles collide harder and more
frequently. This increases the pressure
cards.newFront: Explain why heating a gas (at constant volume) increases its pressure (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Particles gain average kinetic energy and move faster
  • They collide with the walls more frequently and harder (greater force)
  • Greater force per unit area → pressure increases

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
Explain how changing the volume of a
gas affects the pressure of the gas
cards.oldBack:
Volume and pressure are inversely proportional
assuming temperature and mass of the gas is kept
constant. Therefore as volume decreases(gas is
compressed) pressure increases; as volume
increases(gas is expanded) pressure decreases
cards.newFront: How does changing the volume of a gas affect its pressure (at constant temperature)?
cards.newBack:
• Pressure and volume are inversely proportional (p1V1 = p2V2)
  • Smaller volume (compressed): particles collide more frequently → pressure increases
  • Larger volume (expanded): fewer collisions per second → pressure decreases

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
State 2 assumptions you should make while
using P<sub>1</sub> x V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub> x V<sub>2</sub>
cards.oldBack:
- Fixed mass(number of molecules)
- Fixed Temperature
cards.newFront:
State 2 assumptions you should make while
using P<sub>1</sub> x V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub> x V<sub>2</sub>
cards.newBack:
- Fixed mass(number of molecules)
- Fixed Temperature

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
In a bicycle pump, how does pressing
the piston lead to an increase in the
temperature inside the piston?
cards.oldBack:
● Pressing the piston leads to a decrease in volume
● This leads to an increase in pressure
● The particles collide more frequently
● The velocity of the particles increases
● Therefore their temperature will increase
cards.newFront: Why does compressing air in a bicycle pump raise its temperature? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Pressing the piston does work on the gas as volume decreases
  • Transfers energy to the gas particles → their average kinetic energy increases
  • Higher average kinetic energy means a higher temperature

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define electric motor
cards.oldBack:
A current-carrying coil of wire in a magnetic field. The two sides of the coil
that are perpendicular to the magnetic field experience forces in opposite directions, causing
rotation.
cards.newFront: How does a simple d.c. electric motor rotate? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• A current-carrying coil sits in a magnetic field
  • Current flows in opposite directions on opposite sides of the coil
  • The two sides experience forces in opposite directions (motor effect), causing rotation

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define generator effect
cards.oldBack:
When there is relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field, a voltage is induced across the ends of the conductor.

A current will flow if this conductor is part of a complete circuit.
cards.newFront: Define the generator effect (electromagnetic induction) (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field (cutting field lines) induces a voltage
  • An induced current flows if the conductor is part of a complete circuit

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define induced magnet
cards.oldBack:
A material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in an existing
magnetic field, but loses its magnetism quickly once it is removed. Induced magnetism
always produces attractive forces.
cards.newFront: Define an induced magnet (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• A magnetic material that becomes magnetised when placed in a magnetic field
  • Loses its magnetism quickly when removed from the field
  • Always produces an attractive force

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: What are magnetically soft materials?
cards.oldBack:
Materials that can be temporarily
magnetised by an external magnetic field, but can get demagnetised when the external field is removed. Examples include alloys with lower amounts of iron.
cards.newFront: What are magnetically soft materials? Give an example.
cards.newBack:
• Easy to magnetise and easy to demagnetise (temporary magnets)
  • Example: soft iron (used in electromagnet cores and transformers)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
How can you produce a uniform
magnetic field?
cards.oldBack: By placing opposite poles of two magnets across each other, you can create a uniform magnetic field where magnetic field lines are separated with a fixed distance between 2 magnets.
cards.newFront: How do you produce a uniform magnetic field?
cards.newBack:
• Place opposite poles (N and S) of two flat magnets facing each other
  • Field lines between them are straight, parallel and equally spaced

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
How is a plotting compass used to map
out a magnetic field?
cards.oldBack:
● Place a compass (containing a needle magnet) on a piece of paper near the field
● Move the compass to different places on the paper
● Draw an arrow in each position in the same direction as the needle points
● Once you have gathered enough data, you can join the arrows to make a complete field pattern
cards.newFront: How do you use a plotting compass to map a magnetic field? (4 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Place the magnet on paper and put a plotting compass near one pole
  • Mark a dot at the tip of the needle, then move the tail of the needle to that dot
  • Repeat to trace a line from North pole to South pole
  • Join the dots with a smooth curve and add an arrow from N → S

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: What is the motor effect and what causes it?
cards.oldBack:
A current carrying wire placed in a magnetic field experiences a force that pushes the wire.

The force is caused by the field of the current carrying wire interacting with the other magnetic field.
cards.newFront: What is the motor effect and what causes it?
cards.newBack:
• A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force
  • Caused by the interaction between the wire’s magnetic field and the external magnetic field

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: How do loudspeakers work?
cards.oldBack:
● A cone is attached to a coil with an alternating current placed in a magnetic field
● The motor effect causes a force that pushes/pulls the wire/cone, causing it to move in different directions.
● Due to the alternating current, the force causes the cone to vibrate
● This causes pressure variations in the air (sound waves)
cards.newFront: Explain how a loudspeaker works (4 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Alternating current (a.c.) flows through a coil attached to a cone inside a magnetic field
  • The motor effect produces a force on the coil/cone
  • Because the current reverses, the force reverses direction → the cone vibrates
  • Vibrating cone creates sound waves (pressure variations) in the air

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
How is electromagnetic induction used in
alternators to generate alternating
current?
cards.oldBack:
A coil of wire rotates in a magnetic field. The
end of this coil is connected to slip rings which
will cause the current to change direction while
rotating. This means a.c is produced.
cards.newFront: How does an alternator generate alternating current (a.c.)? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• A coil rotates inside a magnetic field, cutting field lines to induce a voltage
  • Each side moves up then down every half turn, so the induced current reverses direction
  • Connected via slip rings → outputs a.c.

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What is the shape of the magnetic field
created around a straight wire when a
current is running through?
cards.oldBack: It is circular.
cards.newFront:
What is the shape of the magnetic field
created around a straight wire when a
current is running through?
cards.newBack:
• Concentric circles centred on the wire (closer together near the wire where field is stronger)
  • Direction found with the Right-Hand Grip Rule (thumb = conventional current + → −)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define half-life (two ways)
cards.oldBack:
The time it takes for the number of unstable nuclei of an isotope in a sample to
halve, or the time it takes for the initial count rate of a sample of the isotope to halve. It is
different for different isotopes.
cards.newFront: Define half-life (2 equivalent definitions)
cards.newBack:
• Time taken for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay
  • OR: time taken for the activity / count rate of a sample to halve
  • Constant for a given isotope (different for different isotopes)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: Define nuclear fission
cards.oldBack:
The splitting of a large and unstable nucleus into two smaller and more
stable nuclei to produce energy. This is the method currently used in nuclear power stations.
cards.newFront: Define nuclear fission
cards.newBack:
• The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) into two smaller daughter nuclei
  • Releases energy and 2–3 neutrons (used in nuclear power stations)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What is the relative masses of a proton,
neutron and electron?
cards.oldBack:
● Proton: 1 
● Neutron: 1 
● Electron: roughly 1/2000
cards.newFront:
What is the relative masses of a proton,
neutron and electron?
cards.newBack:
● Proton: 1
● Neutron: 1
● Electron: roughly 1/2000

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
Describe 3 sources of background
radiation.
cards.oldBack:
- Unstable nuclei in rocks (also give out radon gas)
- Radiation used in medicine
- Some is released from food and water
- Living things (plants can absorb radioactive material as they grow and this can be passed on to the animals that eat them)
- Cosmic rays from the sun
cards.newFront: Give 3 sources of background radiation
cards.newBack:
• Rocks & soil (especially radon gas)
  • Cosmic rays from space
  • Medical uses (X-rays, radiotherapy) · food & drink · nuclear fallout

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
Order the types of ionising radiations
starting with the least ionising to most
ionising
cards.oldBack: Gamma → Beta → Alpha
cards.newFront:
Order the types of ionising radiations
starting with the least ionising to most
ionising
cards.newBack: Gamma → Beta → Alpha

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
Order the types of ionising radiation,
starting with the most penetrating first.
cards.oldBack: Gamma → Beta → Alpha
cards.newFront:
Order the types of ionising radiation,
starting with the most penetrating first.
cards.newBack: Gamma → Beta → Alpha

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What effect does beta minus decay have
on the mass number and atomic number
of an atom?
cards.oldBack:
● The mass number stays the same as the combined number of neutrons and protons hasn’t changed (one has just turned in the other).

● The atomic number increases since there is one more proton.
cards.newFront: How does beta minus (β<sup>−</sup>) decay change mass number and atomic number?
cards.newBack:
• A neutron turns into a proton + electron (β− particle emitted)
  • Mass number: stays the same
  • Atomic number: increases by 1

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: What is the unit for activity?
cards.oldBack: Becquerel (Bq)
cards.newFront: What is the unit for activity?
cards.newBack: Becquerel (Bq)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: How do smoke alarms work?
cards.oldBack:
● A radioactive substance in the alarm emits alpha radiation
● Alpha ionises air in the detector,  causing a current to flow between the plates
● Smoke interferes with the radiation; air is no longer ionised and so no current can flow
● This reduction in current flow triggers the alarm
cards.newFront: Explain how a smoke alarm uses alpha radiation (4 steps)
cards.newBack:
• An alpha source inside the detector ionises air between two plates
  • Ions allow a steady small current to flow
  • Smoke absorbs alpha particles → air is no longer ionised → current drops
  • Drop in current triggers the alarm

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
How is beta radiation used to determine
thickness?
cards.oldBack:
● A beta source is placed above the material and a detector is placed below it

● If a lot of radiation is detected by the detector, too much radiation is passing through the material, and so it is too thin

● If only a little radiation is detected, then the material blocks too much radiation, and so it is too thick
cards.newFront: How is beta radiation used to control material thickness? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Beta source on one side of the sheet, detector on the other
  • High count rate → sheet is too thin (rollers move slightly apart)
  • Low count rate → sheet is too thick (rollers press closer together)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What precautions should people take
when using ionising radiation?
cards.oldBack:
● Avoid handling the source directly (use tongs)
● Wear radiation protective clothing
● Keep the radiation in lead containers to reduce the amount of radiation that can escape
● Avoid being exposed to the radiation for long periods of time
cards.newFront: Give 4 safety precautions when handling radioactive sources
cards.newBack:
• Handle with long tongs (never touch directly; keep distance)
  • Keep exposure time as short as possible
  • Store in lead-lined containers
  • Wear protective clothing / use lead shielding and point away from people

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What is the difference between
contamination and irradiation?
cards.oldBack:
● Contamination is when radioactive substances are transferred to objects through processes such as touching the source or breathing it in

● Irradiation is when the object comes in contact with the radioactive source. The source doesn’t actually enter your body and the radiation will stop if you move away from the area.
cards.newFront: State the difference between contamination and irradiation
cards.newBack:
• Contamination: unwanted radioactive atoms get onto or inside an object/body (keeps emitting radiation until removed/decayed)
  • Irradiation: an object is exposed to radiation from an external source (stops as soon as you move away or shield it)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What is a radioactive tracer used for in
medicine?
cards.oldBack:
● The tracer is placed inside the body (it can be in a drink, eaten or injected)

● The tracer releases gamma radiation which is detected by a detector which moves around the body

● This can then be used to produce a picture of the patient's body
cards.newFront: How is a radioactive tracer used in medicine? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Gamma-emitting isotope (short half-life) is injected, swallowed or inhaled
  • Gamma rays pass out of the body and are detected by an external gamma camera
  • Tracks blood flow / organ function to produce an image

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
Why can’t nuclear fusion be used as our
energy source?
cards.oldBack:
● On earth we can’t get high temperatures and pressures for nuclear fusion to happen, whilst still being cost effective
● This is because both nuclei are positive therefore a lot of energy is required to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between the two nuclei
cards.newFront: Why is nuclear fusion difficult to use as an energy source on Earth? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Both nuclei are positively charged and strongly repel electrostatically
  • Requires extremely high temperature and pressure to overcome repulsion (hard and expensive to sustain)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
Why does your weight vary across
planets?
cards.oldBack:
● Your weight is dependant on g, since weight = mass x g
● The gravitational field strength (g) of a planet varies depending on the radius and mass of the planet
● This means that your weight will also vary
cards.newFront: Why does your weight change on different planets? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• Weight = mass × g (your mass stays constant)
  • Gravitational field strength (g) varies with a planet’s mass and radius

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: What does our solar system consist of?
cards.oldBack:
● The sun (our star)
● 8 Planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune)
● The planet’s natural satellites (ie. the moon)
● Dwarf planets
● Comets and asteroids
cards.newFront: What objects make up our Solar System? (4–5 items)
cards.newBack:
• The Sun (our star)
  • 8 planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune)
  • Moons (natural satellites)
  • Dwarf planets, asteroids and comets

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
Describe the orbits of moons, planets,
comets and artificial satellites.
cards.oldBack:
·Planets follow a (approximately) circular orbit around the Sun.

·Satellites including moons follow a (approximately) circular orbit around planets.

·Comets follow elliptical orbits around the Sun.
cards.newFront: Describe the orbits of planets, moons and comets (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Planets: nearly circular orbits around the Sun
  • Moons & artificial satellites: nearly circular orbits around planets
  • Comets: highly elliptical orbits around the Sun

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
Describe the transition of the star from
the nebula stage to the main sequence.
cards.oldBack:
● The nebula increases in size until it is pulled in due to its gravity, causing GPE to turn into KE of molecules

● As it gets smaller, particles move faster and collide harder so temperature increases.

● Eventually the nebula will become dense and hot enough to begin fusion
cards.newFront: How does a nebula become a main sequence star? (3 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Gravity pulls a cloud of dust and gas (nebula) together → forms a protostar
  • Particles speed up and collide harder → core becomes hotter and denser
  • Core gets hot enough for nuclear fusion (H → He) to begin → main sequence star

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront:
What occurs in the stage when a star is
a main sequence star?
cards.oldBack:
● The fusion in the star releases energy

● During fusion, main sequence stars mostly turn hydrogen into helium.

● Thermal energy released from fusion causes an outward pressure which balances the inward pressure caused by gravity

● The star is in equilibrium so will not collapse due to gravity or expand due to fusion. It is stable.
cards.newFront: Why is a main sequence star stable? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Nuclear fusion fuses hydrogen into helium, releasing huge energy
  • Creates an outward radiation / thermal pressure
  • Outward pressure balances inward gravitational pull (forces in equilibrium)

cards.subject: physics
cards.oldFront: What is supernova?
cards.oldBack:
After the red supergiant stage the star will
expand and get hotter, eventually it will explode
as a supernova. What is left turns into a neutron
star (or a black hole if it is very large).
cards.newFront: What is a supernova and what remains afterwards? (2 points)
cards.newBack:
• The violent explosion of a red supergiant at the end of its life (scatters heavy elements into space)
  • Leaves behind a dense neutron star — or a black hole if the core is massive enough

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you accurately investigate the motion of a toy car or falling ball? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Measure distance with a metre ruler and time with a stopwatch (or light gates to eliminate human reaction-time error)
  • Repeat readings at each distance and calculate a mean (excluding anomalies)
  • Calculate average speed using v = d ÷ t and plot a distance–time graph

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you investigate force vs extension for a spring, metal wire and rubber band? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Measure original length with a ruler at eye level (avoids parallax error), add slotted masses, and calculate extension = new length − original length
  • Spring: straight line through origin up to elastic limit (obeys Hooke’s law)
  • Rubber band: curved graph (does not obey Hooke’s law); loading & unloading curves differ

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Why is current conserved at a junction in a circuit?
cards.newBack:
• Electric charge is conserved (electrons are neither created nor destroyed)
  • Therefore total current entering a junction = total current leaving the junction

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Why is the voltage the same across components connected in parallel?
cards.newBack:
• Each parallel branch connects directly across the same two points of the power supply
  • Every coulomb of charge transfers the same energy across each branch → voltage is identical across every branch

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: State the 3 rules for calculating resistance, current and voltage for two resistors in series
cards.newBack:
• Total resistance: Rtotal = R1 + R2
  • Current: I = Vsupply ÷ Rtotal (same through both resistors)
  • Individual voltages: V1 = I R1 and V2 = I R2 (and V1 + V2 = Vsupply)

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: What 2 boundary behaviours are shared by ALL waves (light, sound, water, EM)?
cards.newBack:
• Reflection: waves bounce off a boundary with angle of incidence = angle of reflection
  • Refraction: waves change speed (and direction if entering at an angle) when crossing into a different medium/depth

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you trace a refracted ray through a glass block or prism? (3 steps)
cards.newBack:
• Draw around the block on paper and shine a narrow beam from a ray box
  • Mark incident and emergent rays with pencil crosses, remove block, and join entry & exit points
  • Draw a normal (at 90°) where the ray meets the boundary and measure i and r from the normal with a protractor

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you find the refractive index (n) of glass accurately using a graph?
cards.newBack:
• Measure pairs of angle of incidence (i) and angle of refraction (r) for 5+ different angles
  • Plot sin i (y-axis) against sin r (x-axis) → straight line through the origin
  • Gradient of the line = refractive index n (n = sin i ÷ sin r)

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Core practical: give a classic experiment to demonstrate conduction, convection and radiation
cards.newBack:
• Conduction: pins waxed along rods of different metals heated at one end (copper drops pins first)
  • Convection: potassium manganate(VII) crystal heated at bottom of water beaker shows purple rising/sinking loop
  • Radiation: compare cooling of matt black vs shiny silver cans of hot water (matt black cools fastest)

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: How does conservation of energy link GPE, KE and work done?
cards.newBack:
Assuming negligible air resistance / friction:
  • Falling object: GPE lost = KE gained (mgh = ½mv2)
  • Force moving an object: work done (W = Fd) = energy transferred (gain in GPE or KE)

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you measure the density of regular solids, irregular solids and liquids?
cards.newBack:
Always measure mass on a top-pan balance, then use ρ = m ÷ V:
  • Regular solid: measure l, w, h with ruler/callipers (V = l × w × h)
  • Irregular solid: find volume by water displacement (measuring cylinder or eureka can)
  • Liquid: mass = (cylinder + liquid) − empty cylinder; read volume at bottom of meniscus

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: How does pressure act at a point inside a liquid or gas at rest?
cards.newBack:
• Acts equally in all directions at any given depth
  • Increases with depth (h) and fluid density (ρ) (p = ρgh)

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Core practical: how do you investigate the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Measure the background count rate first (with no source) and subtract it from every reading
  • Place absorbers in turn between source and GM tube: paper, thin aluminium (few mm), thick lead
  • Count drop shows: α stopped by paper; β stopped by aluminium; γ greatly reduced by thick lead

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: How do you balance a nuclear decay equation?
cards.newBack:
• Total mass number (top) must be equal on both sides
  • Total atomic number / charge (bottom) must be equal on both sides
  • Key symbols: α = 42He · β− = 0−1e · neutron = 10n

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: How do you find half-life from a decay curve or activity data? (3 points)
cards.newBack:
• Subtract background count first (if given)
  • From a graph: read the time for activity to halve (e.g. 800 → 400 Bq); check a second halving (400 → 200 Bq) and average
  • Calculation: count how many halvings occur (A0 → A0/2 → A0/4…) and multiply by one half-life

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Name 3 nuclear processes that can act as sources of energy
cards.newBack:
• Nuclear fission (used in nuclear power stations)
  • Nuclear fusion (powers the Sun and stars)
  • Radioactive decay (e.g. powers deep-space probes & geothermal heat)

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Compare nuclear fission and nuclear fusion
cards.newBack:
• Fission: splitting a large unstable nucleus (e.g. U-235) into smaller daughter nuclei + neutrons (used in nuclear reactors)
  • Fusion: joining two small light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen → helium) at extreme temperature & pressure (powers stars)

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Why does gravitational field strength (g) differ on different planets and moons?
cards.newBack:
• g depends on the mass (larger mass → larger g) and radius of the planet/moon
  • Earth: ~10 N/kg · Moon: ~1.6 N/kg (much smaller mass) · Jupiter: much larger than Earth

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: How is a star’s colour related to its surface temperature?
cards.newBack:
• Hotter stars appear blue / white (emit more short-wavelength light)
  • Cooler stars appear orange / red
  • Order from hottest to coolest: blue → white → yellow → orange → red

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: In the investigating motion practical, why are light gates better than a handheld stopwatch?
cards.newBack:
• Light gates eliminate human reaction-time error (~0.2 s)
  • Measure very short time intervals with much higher resolution and accuracy

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: If a 4 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in series across a 20 V supply, find the current and each resistor’s voltage
cards.newBack:
• Total resistance: R = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω
  • Current: I = V ÷ R = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 A (same in both)
  • Voltages: V1 = 2 × 4 = 8 V · V2 = 2 × 6 = 12 V (check: 8 + 12 = 20 V)

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: What changes — and what stays the same — when a wave refracts into a slower medium?
cards.newBack:
• Speed decreases and wavelength decreases
  • Frequency stays constant (set only by the wave source)

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: In the refraction practical, where must you measure angles i and r from?
cards.newBack: • Always measure angles i and r from the normal (the dashed line drawn at 90° to the surface), never from the glass edge

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: A ball falls from rest. Ignoring air resistance, how do you find its speed just before hitting the ground from its starting height h?
cards.newBack:
• Set GPE lost = KE gained: mgh = ½mv2
  • Mass m cancels → v = √(2gh) (speed doesn’t depend on mass!)

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Why does water spurt further out of a hole near the bottom of a tall tank than from a hole near the top?
cards.newBack:
• Liquid pressure increases with depth (p = ρgh) because of the greater weight of liquid above
  • Pressure acts equally in all directions, pushing water sideways out of the lower hole with greater force

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: In the radiation penetration practical, why must you subtract the background count rate and take repeat readings?
cards.newBack:
• Subtract background: ensures you only measure radiation from the source, not natural background
  • Repeat & average: radioactive decay is random, so averaging gives a more accurate count rate

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Where does the energy released in fission, fusion and radioactive decay come from?
cards.newBack: • Transferred from the nuclear energy store of atomic nuclei into kinetic energy of the products and thermal / radiation energy

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Why is an astronaut’s weight smaller on the Moon than on Earth, even though their mass is unchanged?
cards.newBack:
• Mass is the amount of matter (stays constant everywhere)
  • The Moon has much smaller mass → smaller gravitational field strength g (~1.6 vs ~10 N/kg), so W = mg is smaller

cards.subject: physics
cards.newFront: Which star has a higher surface temperature: a blue-white star or a red giant? Explain briefly.
cards.newBack:
• A blue-white star has a much higher surface temperature
  • Hotter stars emit more high-frequency / short-wavelength blue light; cooler stars peak in longer-wavelength red light
